conceptTags: Linear Regression: Gradient Decomposition, the Normal Equation, and Deep Linear Factorization
stem: Why can training every layer of a deep linear network not be treated as ordinary convex linear regression, even though the overall mapping is linear?

choices.text: Multiplying linear matrices automatically introduces nonlinear activations, so the overall input–output mapping is no longer linear.
Layer weights enter the loss through products, coupling parameters and allowing nonunique factorizations despite a linear map.
Because each layer has a convex subproblem when the others are fixed, optimizing all layers jointly must also be convex.
Depth reduces the sample count and therefore makes regression nonconvex.

explanation: The product \(W^L\cdots W^0\) defines a linear mapping, but it is a multilinear product of the component layer parameters. Scale and factorization are nonunique, and updates to different layers depend on one another, so optimization in parameter space is generally nonconvex. Expanding the gradient gives \(\nabla L=(2/P)(XX^\mathrm{T}w-Xy)\). Thus \(-\nabla L\) contains \(+(2\eta /P)\)Xy and \(-(2\eta /P)XX^\mathrm{T}w\). The first term writes input-target coactivity into the weights; the second grows with the current weights and input covariance, providing stabilization. Its form resembles biological Hebbian learning, but a target y, batch access, and signed error are not ordinary local coactivity.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: A composition of linear maps is linear; the factorized parameterization causes the optimization issue.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Separate convexity does not imply joint convexity; products couple changes across layers.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Depth does not change sample count; squared loss can remain convex in the overall linear map.

conceptTags: Backpropagation: Layerwise Chain Rules, Error Coordinates, and Weight Gradients
stem: Why does the backpropagated error recurrence use the transpose of the downstream weight matrix?

choices.text: Transposition inverts the forward weights, so backpropagation reconstructs the original inputs.
Both passes compute neural activity, so the original weight matrix suffices and transposition is only needed when drawing the network.
The chain rule uses the transpose to sum downstream sensitivities back into gradients of hidden coordinates.
Transposition is valid only for orthogonal weight matrices; all other networks require matrix inversion to apply the chain rule.

explanation: The forward map W carries hidden coordinates into downstream coordinates. The chain rule must aggregate downstream scalar sensitivities back into each hidden coordinate, which is exactly the reverse Jacobian product \(W^\mathrm{T}\delta\); its shape also returns from the downstream dimension to the hidden dimension. Each weight \(W^{(\ell -1)}_{ij}\) contributes presynaptic activation \(z^{(\ell -1)}_j\) to postsynaptic preactivation \(h^{(\ell )}_i\). Therefore \(\partial L/\partial W_{ij}=\delta _{i} z_{j}\), and the complete matrix gradient is the outer product \(\delta ^{(\ell )}(z^{(\ell -1)})^\mathrm{T}\). Batch training averages these outer products.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: A transpose is generally not an inverse; backpropagation computes derivatives rather than reconstructing inputs.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: The backward pass propagates sensitivities, with a different summation direction and matching transpose dimensions.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Jacobian-transpose gradient propagation requires neither orthogonality nor invertibility.

conceptTags: How the Weight Changes Along One Loss Curve
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “How the Weight Changes Along One Loss Curve”?

choices.text: Following the negative gradient guarantees that every step lowers loss and reaches the global minimum, regardless of the chosen learning rate.
Shrinking gaps between markers prove that the optimizer reduces its learning rate after every update.
The markers are biological measurements that determine real synaptic learning speed.
The steps show negative-gradient descent with a suitable learning rate; oversized steps can still raise loss.

explanation: The horizontal axis is the adjustable weight \(w\), not time; the vertical axis is prediction loss \(L(w)=\frac12(w-2)^2\). Curve points are calculated from this formula. The letters mark successive positions: A is \((w,L)=(0,2)\), B is \((1,0.5)\), and C is \((1.5,0.125)\). At A, the slope is \(w-2=-2\). With a fixed learning rate \(\eta=0.5\), the weight increases by \(-0.5\times(-2)=1\), reaching B; recalculating the slope gives the next update to C. Curve height measures how wrong the prediction is; the local slope determines which way to change the weight. The dashed line connects calculated updates; it is neither another loss function nor neural experimental data.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: The direction is local; large steps can invalidate the first-order approximation and increase loss.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Smaller gradients also shrink steps at a fixed learning rate, so marker spacing alone cannot establish a schedule.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: These points are calculated from the example loss and learning rate, without neural experimental data or a biological time unit.

conceptTags: Visual Hierarchy, the LNP Model, and Center-Surround Computation
stem: Why is “ON cells prefer light and OFF cells prefer dark” an incomplete account of a center-surround receptive field?

choices.text: ON and OFF labels specify different luminance thresholds, while center and surround illumination always have the same sign of effect within a cell.
Responses also depend on whether contrast falls in the center or surround; balanced positive and negative regions can cancel uniform luminance changes.
Equal receptive-field area guarantees equal responses, regardless of weight signs or arrangement.
Uniform brightening makes both ON-center and surround contributions positive, so it always produces the largest possible response regardless of spatial contrast.

explanation: The response depends on contrast location and surround context. A bright spot in an ON center can excite, whereas a bright surround can cancel it. A balanced kernel may not respond to the same global luminance, so both polarity and spatial pattern must be specified. Place photoreceptors, retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), V1, MT, IT, and LIP on a hierarchy diagram. The retina first encodes local contrast; V1 emphasizes local structure such as orientation; MT and the dorsal stream are associated with motion and action-relevant variables; IT and the ventral stream with object features; and LIP often with decision-related representations. This computational map does not imply exclusively one-way feedforward information flow.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Center and surround carry opposing filter weights, which a single luminance threshold cannot describe.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Responses depend on matching the signed kernel, not area alone.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The antagonistic surround contributes with the opposite sign and can cancel center drive.

conceptTags: Feature Maps, Gabor Simple Cells, and Orientation Tuning
stem: Why does changing Gabor phase \(\phi\) not change preferred orientation \(\theta\)?

choices.text: Phase only changes response gain, without moving lobes or changing how bright and dark regions align with the filter.
Phase and orientation rotate the entire coordinate system through the same angle; they differ only in the units used to express that angle.
Phase shifts bright and dark lobes along a fixed axis; orientation rotates that axis, changing a different spatial property.
Changing phase increases spatial frequency and rotates the preferred orientation.

explanation: \(\phi\) translates positive and negative lobes along a fixed carrier axis and determines whether a bright or dark edge aligns with the filter. \(\theta\) rotates the coordinate system and determines which edge or grating direction aligns with the elongated lobes. V1 simple-cell receptive fields often contain alternating elongated ON and OFF lobes. A Gabor kernel uses a Gaussian envelope to localize position and size and a cosine carrier to create the alternating lobes. \(\theta\) rotates the coordinates, k controls spatial frequency, and \(\phi\) controls phase. Orientation tuning arises because positive contributions add when an edge aligns with the lobes, whereas an orthogonal edge straddles positive and negative regions and cancels.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Phase changes the carrier's bright and dark positions and therefore their alignment.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Phase shifts the carrier pattern; orientation rotates spatial coordinates, so they are distinct transformations.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Spatial frequency controls lobe spacing; phase alone changes neither that frequency nor the axis orientation.

conceptTags: Spatiotemporal Receptive Fields and Motion as Space-Time Orientation
stem: Why does a biphasic temporal kernel not automatically guarantee direction selectivity?

choices.text: The positive temporal lobe encodes rightward motion and the negative lobe encodes leftward motion, so two signs already establish direction selectivity.
Every biphasic temporal kernel automatically shifts spatial lobes over delays, making a separable kernel equivalent to a tilted space–time kernel.
A sufficiently narrow temporal kernel distinguishes opposite directions by itself.
A biphasic temporal kernel can reweight one fixed spatial pattern; direction selectivity also needs specific pairings of locations and delays.

explanation: If the kernel still factors into a fixed spatial profile and a temporal waveform, it only reweights one spatial feature over time and never pairs distinct locations with particular lags. Direction selectivity requires space-time nonseparability or an equivalent multichannel nonlinear computation. A vertical edge moving rightward at velocity v satisfies \(x(t)=x_{0}+vt\). In an x-t diagram it is an oblique line of slope \(dx/dt=v\). If the positive lobes of a receptive field lie along the same line, the edge traverses every positive zone in sequence and produces a large inner product. An edge moving the other way follows the opposite slope and encounters mismatched positive and negative zones.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Temporal weight signs do not specify left versus right; spatial positions must also be paired with delays.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: A separable kernel only rescales its fixed spatial profile at each delay; preferred positions do not move.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Higher temporal resolution alone does not establish the spatial ordering needed to distinguish direction.

conceptTags: From ON/OFF Local-Contrast Channels to an Oriented Gabor-Like Receptive Field
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “From ON/OFF Local-Contrast Channels to an Oriented Gabor-Like Receptive Field”?

choices.text: ON/OFF channels extract contrast; aligned signed subfields make matching orientations add coherently, producing orientation selectivity.
A circularly symmetric DoG already specifies a preferred orientation; subsequent spatial arrangement changes only gain and leaves selectivity unchanged.
Summing the total ON and OFF activity gives the same orientation tuning regardless of subfield positions, signs, or alignment along an axis.
The feature maps copy absolute luminance rather than transforming the image.

explanation: ON/OFF center-surround filters first recode absolute luminance as local contrast. Arranging several polarity-specific subfields along one axis makes signed contributions add for the matching direction and cancel for an orthogonal direction, creating an elongated, orientation-selective Gabor-like linear receptive field. The diagram distinguishes local DoG contrast computation from the later subfield arrangement that creates orientation tuning.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: A circular kernel has no preferred orientation; elongated arrangements break rotational symmetry.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Orientation tuning depends on matching the signed spatial arrangement, so those details cannot be discarded.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Feature maps represent filter matches and local contrast, not copies of pixel intensity.

conceptTags: White-Noise System Identification in Three Notations
stem: Why must each member of the spike-triggered ensemble contain a stimulus history rather than only the frame in which the spike occurs?

choices.text: Current frames always contain future information, and histories only remove it.
A history vector repeats the current frame to increase sample count, and more repetitions independently identify each lag's contribution.
Spikes have latency and can depend on several past moments; stimulus histories preserve temporal structure that the current frame may miss.
Responses depend only on the current frame, so past frames merely smooth measurement noise and cannot change the estimated temporal structure.

explanation: Neural responses have latency and may depend on multiple past lags. Using only the current frame discards temporal filtering and attaches the causal feature to the wrong spike time. A history vector permits simultaneous estimation of spatial and temporal receptive-field structure. System identification reverses forward prediction. A forward LNP model predicts spikes from known K and F; the experiment supplies stimulus s and spikes k and seeks K and F. A standard protocol presents random checkerboard white noise, records neural spikes, looks backward from every spike over the same time lags, and averages those stimulus histories. Stimulus coordinates, frame duration, and neural latency must be defined first.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: A current frame need not contain future information; earlier stimulation may drive the spike through temporal filtering.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Histories need actual past frames; repeating one frame adds no independent information about temporal filtering.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Latency and integration across past moments are part of the receptive field being estimated, not merely measurement noise.

conceptTags: Least Squares, the Hessian, and White-Noise Isotropy
stem: Why does an elongated loss contour indicate that some filter combinations are estimated unreliably?

choices.text: The long axis has the largest Hessian eigenvalue, so tiny parameter changes create large losses and therefore make that direction least reliable.
Elongated contours prove that the spatial receptive field itself is elongated.
Every filter along the long axis makes exactly identical predictions with zero loss, so an elongated contour always implies a nonunique solution.
Low curvature along the long axis lets different filters predict similarly, so noise can move the estimate far in that direction.

explanation: Moving along the ellipse's long axis raises loss only slightly. This is a small-eigenvalue direction of the Hessian, where many different K values make similar predictions on the sampled stimuli, allowing finite noise to shift the minimum substantially. For a linear model with quadratic loss, the Hessian \(H=SS^\mathrm{T}/T\) is independent of K. Its eigenvectors are the principal axes of the loss ellipse and its eigenvalues are curvatures. Along a large-eigenvalue direction, a small change in K noticeably changes predictions and the data tightly constrain the minimum. Along a small-eigenvalue direction, the loss is flat and recording noise, finite samples, or regularization can move the estimate substantially.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: At a fixed loss increment, the long axis corresponds to small curvature and weak constraints.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: These contours describe parameter-space loss, not the receptive field's shape in visual space.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: A small nonzero eigenvalue can produce a unique but unstable estimate; strict nonuniqueness requires missing constraints.

conceptTags: From the Kernel Estimate to the STA, Nonlinearity, and Failure Diagnostics
stem: Why is a smooth increasing \(\hat{F}(L)\) curve on the training data insufficient evidence that an LNP model predicts?

choices.text: The filter and curve fitted to the same data may absorb noise; freeze the model and test spike predictions on held-out stimuli.
A strictly monotonic training curve removes all noise, so it eliminates the need for held-out evaluation.
Refit both the filter and nonlinearity on test spikes, then use those same spikes to demonstrate that the resulting model generalizes.
Matching the overall mean firing rate guarantees correct stimulus-specific predictions.

explanation: Both K and F were estimated from the same data, and binning plus a flexible curve can absorb noise. Generalization must be tested by computing projections on held-out stimuli and predicting conditional rates or spikes there. After estimating \(\hat{K}\), compute \(L_{t}=\hat{K}^\mathrm{T}s_{t}\) in every time bin, group values into bins of L, and estimate empirical \(P(\mathrm{spike}|L)\). The small-bin Poisson approximation gives \(P(k=1|L)\approx \Delta tF(L)\), hence \(\hat{F}(L)=P(\mathrm{spike}|L)/\Delta t\). Finally combine \(\hat{K}\), \(\hat{F}\), and the Poisson stage on held-out stimuli and compare predicted with observed spikes; a training STA alone is not a model test.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Monotonicity or smoothness can still permit overfitting and does not establish prediction on new data.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Refitting to test responses uses the answers being evaluated and destroys independence of the prediction test.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: A correct overall mean can coexist with large errors in conditional responses.

conceptTags: Forward LNP Prediction and Reverse STA Estimation Form One Validation Workflow
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Forward LNP Prediction and Reverse STA Estimation Form One Validation Workflow”?

choices.text: Looking backward from spikes means future stimuli cause current responses, making STA an acausal encoding model.
Forward LNP predicts spikes; reverse averaging estimates the filter direction when the white Gaussian single-feature STA is nonzero.
The STA–filter relation holds for all stimulus distributions and even nonlinearities, and sufficient sampling always guarantees a nonzero STA that recovers the complete filter.
The STA alone determines the nonlinearity, noise distribution, and all future predictions.

explanation: A forward LNP model projects stimulus history onto \(L=k^{\mathrm{T}}s\), transforms it through \(F(L)\) into a conditional firing rate, and generates spikes. Reverse analysis aligns and averages the stimulus history before each spike. For zero-mean white Gaussian input, one relevant dimension, and sufficient data, STA points along k. Colored input, an even nonlinearity, or multiple relevant dimensions breaks this simple relation.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Reverse analysis describes an estimation procedure using earlier stimuli, not a reversal of physiological causality.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Colored inputs can bias the STA, while even responses can cancel it even with abundant data.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The STA primarily supplies directional information; nonlinearity, scale, and predictive validation require separate treatment.

conceptTags: Multiple Relevant Features and Spike-Triggered Covariance
stem: Why cannot the sign of an STC eigenvector say whether a stimulus is excitatory or inhibitory?

choices.text: Positive eigenvectors are excitatory and negative ones inhibitory, provided the numerical solver uses a consistent sign convention.
A positive eigenvalue guarantees monotonically increasing firing on both sides of its axis, while a negative eigenvalue guarantees decreasing firing on both sides.
Covariance retains only the stimulus mean and therefore loses response polarity.
An eigenvector's overall sign is arbitrary: covariance identifies an axis, while the response nonlinearity determines preferences for signed projections.

explanation: Covariance describes an unoriented axis. v and -v have identical squared projections and covariance. To learn how projection sign affects rate, fit or inspect the nonlinearity along that axis. Use the blowfly H1 neuron as an example: its stimulus \(s(t)=v(t)\) is image velocity rather than a two-dimensional light pattern. The response may depend on projections through several temporal filters \(K_{1}\cdots K_{n}\) followed by a multidimensional nonlinearity F. Thus stimulus-vector coordinates are defined by the question: they may be pixels, velocity history, past spikes, or other measured covariates.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: A solver's sign choice has no physiological meaning; reversing the vector leaves the same feature axis.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Eigenvalue sign describes conditional variance expansion or contraction, not the complete rate-versus-projection function.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Covariance describes centered second-order statistics; the relevant issue is the arbitrary sign of the axis.

conceptTags: The Three GLM Components and Gaussian and Poisson Likelihoods
stem: Why is the identity link \(\lambda =\eta\) structurally unsuitable for \(a \operatorname{Poisson} GLM\)?

choices.text: An unconstrained linear predictor may be negative; using it directly as the expected count can violate the Poisson mean's allowed range.
An identity link forces every observed count to equal its mean and removes Poisson randomness.
The problem is that an identity link allows means above one, whereas every Poisson mean must stay between zero and one like a binary probability.
A log link automatically fixes all count-window and physical-unit errors.

explanation: The linear predictor \(\eta\) may be any real number, so an identity link permits negative expected counts. The log link \(\lambda =e^\eta\) maps the whole real line to positive means and yields the convenient residual gradient of the canonical Poisson likelihood. For a unit-variance Gaussian model with identity link, \(m=\eta =x^\mathrm{T}\beta\). The β-dependent part of the log likelihood is \(-1/2\Sigma (y-m)^2\), so likelihood maximization equals mean-squared-error minimization. Unknown or heteroscedastic variance requires an extension; squared loss is not the only model for continuous responses.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: The link specifies a mean, not a deterministic equality between each observation and that mean.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Expected counts can exceed one; the issue with an unconstrained identity link is negative values.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Binning and units must be specified separately; choosing a link does not correct inconsistent conventions.

conceptTags: Retinal Population Filters, Bernoulli Logit, and Conditional Dependence
stem: Why does fitting stimulus and coupling filters jointly still not justify interpreting a coupling coefficient as a causal synapse?

choices.text: Joint fitting removes all common input, so every nonzero coupling necessarily identifies a direct anatomical connection.
Joint fitting controls included variables only; unobserved common input and indirect paths can still produce coupling without a direct synapse.
If coupling predicts held-out responses consistently, its causal direction and direct connection are established without intervention or additional identifiability assumptions.
Positive coupling always proves excitation; only negative coupling remains ambiguous.

explanation: The model controls only measured covariates. Unobserved common input, global state, model mismatch, and indirect network paths can still create conditional dependence. Establishing a causal synapse additionally requires intervention, anatomy, or stronger identifiability assumptions. In a very small bin, \(y_{t}\in {0,1}\) and a Bernoulli likelihood is suitable. Use log odds \(\theta =\log[q/(1-q)]\) as predictor \(\eta\), with inverse link \(q=e^\eta /(1+e^\eta )\). At \(\eta =0\), \(q=0.5\); increasing \(\eta\) by one multiplies the odds by e. That statement is more accurate than a fixed probability increment because sigmoid slope differs near 0 and near 1.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Unobserved inputs do not disappear simply because other measured covariates are fitted.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Stable prediction can arise from common causes or indirect paths and does not establish direct causation.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Both signs describe conditional predictive relationships and can be influenced by omitted variables.

conceptTags: A Population GLM Places Stimulus, Self-History, and Coupling in One Conditional Predictor
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “A Population GLM Places Stimulus, Self-History, and Coupling in One Conditional Predictor”?

choices.text: Each branch generates independent spikes that are summed, and the inverse link merely sets the plot's axis units.
Self-history and coupling branches may include current and future spikes, improving accuracy without leaking the response because the stimulus is also included in the model.
Stimulus and histories combine in the predictor; the inverse link yields a conditional mean or probability, not an anatomical wiring map.
Including stimulus input turns the coupling branch into a verified anatomical wiring map.

explanation: A population GLM adds a stimulus filter, self-history filter, and cross-neuron coupling filters in predictor \(\eta _{i}(t)\), then uses a log or logit inverse link to produce a nonnegative rate or binary spike probability. Simultaneous fitting reduces omitted-covariate confounding, but a coupling coefficient still denotes predictive dependence conditional on the included variables, not an anatomical synapse.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Branches combine into a linear predictor; the inverse link maps that predictor to a response mean or probability.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Current targets and future events leak information; history covariates must precede the predicted event.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Measured stimulus control cannot eliminate unobserved common drive or indirect interactions.

conceptTags: Barlow's Hypotheses and the Foundations of Information Theory
stem: Why does negative differential entropy not mean probability theory has failed?

choices.text: Densities can exceed one and differential entropy depends on units, so negative values need not violate probability theory.
Negative differential entropy means some event probabilities are negative, which continuous models permit.
The negative sign only comes from using natural logarithms, so changing to base-two logarithms always makes differential entropy nonnegative.
Differential entropy must be nonnegative; a negative result proves that the density is not normalized and the model must be refitted.

explanation: A continuous density is not the probability of one outcome; it may exceed 1, and its entropy contains the coordinate bin size or units. Rescaling a variable adds a log-scale term. Shared scale contributions cancel in MI, which remains nonnegative and retains its dependence interpretation. Barlow's framework contributes three ideas: detect “passwords” of critical significance, filter signals for other nervous-system regions, and recode sensory messages to reduce redundancy. Focus on the third. Efficient coding explains why a code is advantageous under specified input statistics, noise, and cost. It is a normative hypothesis; the same receptive field may also have developmental, biophysical, or task-specific explanations.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Neither probability nor density may be negative; densities, unlike event probabilities, can exceed one.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Changing logarithm base multiplies by a positive factor and does not change the sign.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: A normalized density can have negative differential entropy, for example on an interval shorter than one unit.

conceptTags: The Noisy Retina of Atick and Redlich and Covariance Propagation
stem: Why does moving input and output noise into one term before A change the optimization?

choices.text: Both noises alter only the output mean, so combining them merely removes a constant bias.
Input noise is filtered by the encoder, whereas output noise is added afterward; changing gain affects them differently and changes the optimal tradeoff.
Independence guarantees that moving output noise before the encoder preserves the same output distribution for every candidate gain, without changing the noise model.
Only output noise is amplified by the encoder; input noise bypasses it.

explanation: A reshapes input noise, so increasing gain at one frequency also amplifies its input noise. Output noise does not pass through A, and increasing gain can improve signal relative to output noise. Their effects on the gain tradeoff differ and cannot be merged. Assuming signal and noises are zero-mean and mutually independent, \(C_{x}=C_{s}+C_{\eta _{x}}\). A linear transformation yields \(AC_{x}A^\mathrm{T}\), after which output noise adds: \(C_{y}=A(C_{s}+C_{\eta _{x}})A^\mathrm{T}+C_{\eta _{y}}\). Input noise is amplified or attenuated together with the signal, while output noise never passes through A; optimal gain therefore cannot be based on signal covariance alone.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Zero-mean noises still contribute covariance; their location determines whether that covariance is transformed.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Independence permits covariance addition, not ignoring the intervening transform; equivalent input noise generally depends on the encoder.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The order is reversed: input noise passes through the encoder with the signal, while output noise is added afterward.

conceptTags: Gaussian Information, Nonunique Decorrelation, and the Selection of Center-Surround Filters
stem: What crucial conditions are missing from the statement “decorrelation produces center-surround filters”?

choices.text: Identity output covariance necessarily makes every channel's spatial filter a localized center–surround pattern.
Every orthogonal rotation reintroduces correlations between whitened channels, so decorrelation alone already excludes all nonlocal encoders from the solution set.
Whitened channels can still be orthogonally rotated without changing covariance; local center–surround shapes require symmetry, wiring, or additional constraints.
More samples remove every ambiguity and select a unique center–surround filter.

explanation: Decorrelation requires a diagonal output covariance; whitening additionally scales all variances to one, so any orthogonal rotation preserves the identity covariance. A merely diagonal covariance with unequal variances generally gains off-diagonal entries after rotation. Translation and rotation symmetry, locality, wiring, noise, or cost constraints are still needed to select center-surround filters among the equivalent whitened solutions. A whitening transform V satisfies \(VC_{x}V^\mathrm{T}=I\). For any orthogonal U, \((UV)C_{x}(UV)^\mathrm{T}=UIU^\mathrm{T}=I\), so the pre-output-noise whitened code may be rotated without changing covariance. Full Gaussian MI is also unchanged only if output noise is isotropic, \(C_{\eta _{y}}=\sigma _{y}^{2}I\), or absent; then total and conditional-noise covariances undergo the same orthogonal similarity transformation. With anisotropic output noise, rotating the encoder changes signal alignment with the noise axes and generally changes MI. Decorrelation alone therefore identifies a family of solutions, not a unique localized center-surround shape for each neuron.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Identity covariance constrains statistics but does not uniquely determine each channel's spatial shape.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Identity covariance is invariant under orthogonal rotation, leaving an equivalent family of whitened encoders.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Rotational ambiguity is a symmetry of the objective, not merely finite-sample noise.

conceptTags: Redundancy Reduction in a Noisy Sensory Channel Must Respect Fidelity and Output-Cost Constraints
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Redundancy Reduction in a Noisy Sensory Channel Must Respect Fidelity and Output-Cost Constraints”?

choices.text: Setting every encoder gain to zero is optimal because the channels become uncorrelated, which guarantees preservation of all sensory information.
Output noise passes through the encoder with the signal, so a single fixed input covariance can replace all noise locations throughout optimization.
Whitening uniquely determines each neuron's localized center–surround receptive field.
Signal and input noise pass through the encoder before output noise is added; information and output cost constrain redundancy reduction.

explanation: Encoder A transforms signal and input noise together, whereas output noise enters after A. A diagonal output covariance alone therefore does not guarantee useful coding. In the Atick–Redlich framework, redundancy is reduced subject to retained-information and output-power or dynamic-range constraints. Whitening removes second-order correlations, but any orthogonal rotation preserves whitened covariance; localized center-surround filters require additional assumptions such as symmetry and locality.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Zero gain also removes the signal; absent correlation is not a substitute for information retention.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Output noise is added after the encoder and cannot simply be treated as the same fixed input noise.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Orthogonal rotations leave equivalent whitened codes; localized shapes need additional structural constraints.

conceptTags: SNR Selects the Filtering Objective: Remove Redundancy or Reduce Noise
stem: Why should a weaker surround in low light not be summarized as the visual system “no longer caring about edges”?

choices.text: A weaker surround proves the animal has permanently abandoned edges and will ignore them even after bright-light conditions return.
Unreliable high-frequency evidence favors pooling over differencing, trading resolution for stability without abandoning edges as a goal.
Dim light eliminates every high-frequency signal completely, so all such channels should be deleted and any remaining contrast information has no value.
A weaker surround improves precision without ever sacrificing spatial resolution.

explanation: Edges can remain behaviorally important. The change means that current high-frequency evidence is unreliable relative to noise and strong differencing would amplify noise. The system temporarily sacrifices resolution for a more stable estimate; the behavioral target need not have changed. Interpret filter shape along an SNR axis. At high SNR, input detail is reliable relative to internal and photon noise. Neighboring pixels are then strongly correlated, and transmitting them unchanged wastes limited output dynamic range on repeated information. An excitatory-center, inhibitory-surround difference kernel suppresses common slow components while retaining edges, reducing output correlations. A strong surround is a normative prediction under specified statistics and costs; it does not alone establish its synaptic implementation.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Adaptation reflects present signal and noise conditions, not a demonstrated permanent change in task preferences.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Reliability usually varies continuously across frequencies rather than vanishing everywhere at one threshold.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Pooling can reduce independent noise while also smoothing detail and lowering spatial resolution.

conceptTags: From Translation-Invariant Statistics to Fourier Diagonalization
stem: Why do Fourier modes “diagonalize” a translation-invariant linear filter?

choices.text: Diagonalization converts every input frequency into one output frequency and erases differences between modes.
A Fourier transform diagonalizes every position-dependent linear filter, so translation invariance is unnecessary and arbitrary spatial changes cannot mix frequencies.
Convolution preserves each Fourier mode's frequency and changes only its complex amplitude; modes do not mix, leaving a gain for each frequency.
Real images force all Fourier gains to be positive real numbers.

explanation: After convolution, each input mode \(e^{i\xi \cdot x}\) remains the same \(\xi\) and is multiplied only by complex number \(\hat{K}(\xi )\); distinct \(\xi\) never mix. In this basis, the operator is represented by diagonal gains, one per mode. A two-dimensional component \(e^{i\xi \cdot x}\) carries frequency direction and phase. The dot product \(\xi \cdot x\) projects position onto the frequency vector. Phase changes fastest along \(\xi\) and remains constant in the perpendicular direction, so visible stripes are perpendicular to \(\xi\). A real image uses paired \(+\xi\) and \(-\xi\) components whose imaginary parts cancel. Near the spectrum center are slow variations; farther away are finer spatial structures.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Each mode retains its frequency; diagonalization removes coupling rather than frequency labels.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Position-dependent filters can mix frequencies; the stated diagonal structure relies on convolution or translation invariance.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Real kernels can have complex gains; conjugate symmetry, not positivity of every gain, ensures real outputs.

conceptTags: Natural-Image Power Spectra, Whitening, and Testable Adaptation
stem: Why must an LNP filter's scale convention be fixed before comparing two adaptation conditions?

choices.text: Every filter-amplitude difference is genuine adaptation because the nonlinearity can change only the output baseline.
Fixing the norm forces filter direction and nonlinearity to be identical across conditions, eliminating the need to test adaptation.
Normalization only prevents numerical overflow; with enough samples the data uniquely determine the separate scales of both the filter and nonlinearity without any additional convention.
Rescaling the filter can be offset by reparameterizing the nonlinearity; identical predictions can therefore appear to have different filter gains without a fixed convention.

explanation: Multiplying k by constant a while dividing the nonlinearity's horizontal axis by a gives identical firing predictions. Without fixing ||k|| or another convention, an apparent gain change can be only parameterization nonuniqueness. This turns this prediction into an LNP measurement. Present sufficiently rich stimuli under high and low light or different spatial correlations, estimate filter \(k_{c}\) separately, and then estimate each condition's nonlinearity \(f_{c}\). Fix a normalization before comparing filters—for example \(||k_{c}||=1\) with signs aligned by the dominant lobe—because multiplying k by a constant and inversely scaling the input axis of f gives identical predictions. Then compare spatial profile, Fourier gain, integrated center-surround ratio, and cross-condition prediction.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: The nonlinearity's input scale can also change, compensating for a rescaled filter projection.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Normalization removes one parameter freedom; direction, shape, and nonlinearity may still change.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: The ambiguity is structural, so more samples alone do not remove equivalent parameterizations.

conceptTags: Noise Truncates the Ideal High-Frequency Gain of Natural-Image Whitening
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Noise Truncates the Ideal High-Frequency Gain of Natural-Image Whitening”?

choices.text: Ideal whitening increases gain with frequency; accounting for noise produces high-frequency roll-off, and lower SNR narrows the reliable band further.
The high-frequency roll-off proves natural images contain no high-frequency structure and has nothing to do with optics or noise.
The curves are successive recordings over time from the same neuron.
The lower-SNR curve recommends unlimited amplification of the highest frequencies in dim light to reconstruct every edge perfectly without increasing any noise cost.

explanation: If natural-image power is approximated by \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\) and noise and gain limits are temporarily ignored, flattening \(P_{\mathrm{out}}=|\hat{K}|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}\) requires \(|\hat{K}|\propto |\xi |\). Real optics attenuate extreme high-frequency signal without eliminating approximately flat output noise, so a noise-aware filter rolls off at high frequencies. When SNR falls further, the reliable band narrows and favors pooling. All three curves are normalized theoretical sketches, not empirical measurements.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: High-frequency signals can exist yet be unreliable; roll-off reflects signal, noise, and optical limits.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: The horizontal axis is spatial frequency; the curves are normalized theoretical illustrations, not temporal measurements.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Noise-dominated frequencies should not receive unlimited gain; lower SNR instead favors a narrower band and pooling.

conceptTags: From Simple-Cell Pooling to Complex-Cell Energy
stem: Why does the energy model retain orientation tuning after gaining phase invariance?

choices.text: Orientation changes also rotate the outputs at fixed radius, making their squared sum insensitive to orientation just as it is to phase.
Squaring cannot remove phase, so the energy model has no phase invariance.
Phase redistributes quadrature outputs, but orientation mismatch reduces their shared amplitude and hence the squared energy.
Poisson noise creates orientation tuning even when both filters have identical mean responses to every orientation, so filter selectivity is unnecessary.

explanation: Phase rotates the matched quadrature outputs in their two-dimensional plane. Changing orientation reduces both filter projections' common amplitude A, so \(A^{2}\) still falls with orientation mismatch. This links cascade models to the Hubel–Wiesel construction. If multiple LGN-like center-surround units are arranged along an oblique axis and pooled with same-sign weights, only a light-dark edge matching that arrangement drives many inputs together, producing an elongated simple-cell receptive field. This construction explains the spatial geometry of orientation selectivity but remains sensitive to light-dark position: translating the same grating by half a period reverses the linear projection.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Fixed-radius rotation describes phase changes within matched features; orientation mismatch generally lowers projection amplitude.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: One squared response still varies with phase, but the matched quadrature pair's squared sum can cancel that variation.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Orientation dependence comes from filter matching; Poisson noise does not create a missing mean preference.

conceptTags: Task Optimization and Neural Predictivity Are Two Different Tests
stem: Why is it invalid to repeatedly select the most brain-like network layer on test neural stimuli and report its highest correlation on the same data?

choices.text: Layer selection is not fitting if network weights remain frozen, so the largest test correlation remains an independent performance estimate.
Trying more layers cancels noise and makes the highest correlation unbiased.
Selecting a layer and then recalculating correlation on the same test set removes leakage, provided the layer is fixed during the final calculation and no weights change.
Choosing layers from test responses uses the test data and biases the maximum correlation; select on validation data and evaluate once on an independent test set.

explanation: Repeated layer selection already uses the test responses. The maximum contains positive selection noise and is biased upward. Choose layers and regularization on validation neural data and perform the final evaluation once on an independent test set. High task accuracy does not define neural similarity. Many internal coordinate systems can implement the same classification boundary; networks that rely on texture or shape may score similarly on labels. Predictivity also depends on mapping flexibility. A nonlinear mapper with far more parameters than observations can fit almost any representation to training responses. Use simple mappings of equal complexity and identical cross-validation for every candidate layer.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Data-dependent layer selection is model selection and can exploit test-response noise.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Taking a maximum favors positive noise; more candidates usually increase selection bias.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Recalculation cannot undo earlier use of test answers; independent evaluation data are still needed.

conceptTags: E/I Recurrence, Nullclines, and Inhibition Stabilization
stem: Why does lower inhibitory-neuron firing after surround not imply that inhibition did not cause surround suppression?

choices.text: Rates reflect circuit rebalancing: less excitatory drive can lower inhibitory firing while inhibition still helps produce suppression.
Lower inhibitory firing means all inhibitory synapses have failed, so only intrinsic adaptation in excitatory cells can cause the suppression.
Any decrease in inhibitory firing necessarily increases net input to target cells, regardless of the simultaneous change in excitatory drive.
A lower inhibitory rate alone proves that the network is an ISN.

explanation: A firing rate is the network fixed-point outcome, while inhibitory current also depends on connectivity and presynaptic rate. Surround can first lower E drive and thereby lower I, even though I feedback still determines the fixed point at which E amplification is contained. The ISN has an excitatory subnetwork that would be unstable in isolation—effective recurrent E gain exceeds leak—but fast inhibitory feedback stabilizes the complete E/I network. The name does not mean that inhibitory firing always rises or that every suppression comes from added I input. Under some perturbations, stronger external drive to I lowers its steady-state rate. This paradoxical response arises from network rebalancing and tests ISN structure more directly than simply measuring whether I is large.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Reduced population firing does not mean synapses have failed or exclude inhibition from the circuit response.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Net input depends on both contributions; excitatory drive may decrease more strongly.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: An ISN requires an unstable excitatory subsystem and a stable complete loop; one rate change is insufficient.

conceptTags: After Surround Input Shifts the I-Nullcline, Both E and I Can Fall at the Stable Intersection
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “After Surround Input Shifts the I-Nullcline, Both E and I Can Fall at the Stable Intersection”?

choices.text: Shifting the I-nullcline upward must increase the final inhibitory rate, so the lower surround intersection can only be a plotting error.
The shifted I-nullcline can intersect at lower E and I rates; this identifies a steady state, whose stability still needs checking.
Every nullcline intersection necessarily attracts all nearby trajectories without further analysis.
The lower I rate proves that the additional surround drive is negative and that the excitatory subsystem no longer needs any inhibitory feedback to remain stable.

explanation: In a locally linear E/I rate model, a nullcline intersection is a steady state. Increasing surround drive to the I population shifts the I-nullcline upward. Its new intersection with the fixed E-nullcline can have both lower \(r_{E}\) and lower \(r_{I}\), so surround suppression does not require inhibitory firing to rise. The curves are normalized geometric sketches of the course equations. Full stability still requires Jacobian eigenvalues and cannot be inferred from line intersection alone.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: The joint intersection determines the final rates; movement of one curve is not itself a population-rate change.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: An intersection ensures zero derivatives; local dynamics still determine whether it is stable.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: In an ISN, positive I drive can lower steady-state I firing without removing inhibition's stabilizing role.

conceptTags: Motor Control Is a Brain–Body–Environment Loop
stem: Why does larger proportional gain improve disturbance rejection in a delay-free model but not justify infinite gain in a biological system?

choices.text: The delay-free model already includes all real stability limits, so any positive gain can grow without bound without producing overshoot or oscillation.
Feedback gain changes noise but never affects constant-disturbance steady-state error.
Increasing gain automatically shortens neural conduction time until sufficiently strong feedback eliminates all delay and restores the ideal model.
Real loops also contain sensory delays, muscle dynamics, and noise; high gain can amplify noise and produce overshoot or oscillation.

explanation: The ideal equation omits sensory delay, muscle dynamics, noise, saturation, and energetic cost. High gain amplifies noise and can cause overshoot or oscillation in a delayed loop, so stability must be assessed for the complete loop. Embed the motor system in coupled brain, body, and environment dynamics. Descending pathways change muscle activation; body mechanics convert activation into posture and velocity; gravity, contact, and object reaction forces alter body state; and proprioceptive, visual, and cutaneous signals return the outcome to the nervous system. Every arrow has delay and dynamics. Movement is therefore a time-evolving closed loop, not a static stimulus-response lookup.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Omitting delays and actuator dynamics prevents such a guarantee for the real loop.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Proportional gain changes ideal steady-state error, while real systems impose additional constraints.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Control gain is not conduction speed and cannot automatically remove neural or mechanical delays.

conceptTags: The Recurrent Population Equation and Eigenmode Decomposition
stem: For asymmetric W, why can normalized right eigenvectors not justify writing \(\alpha =V^\mathrm{T} h\)?

choices.text: Unit length does not ensure orthogonality; coordinates require the eigenvector matrix's inverse or left eigenvectors.
Normalizing each eigenvector automatically makes all vectors orthogonal, so transposition and inversion always give the same coordinates.
Right eigenvectors of every asymmetric matrix are linearly dependent, so no eigenbasis coordinate transform or inverse matrix can ever be used.
Distinct eigenvalues guarantee orthogonal right eigenvectors even for asymmetric matrices.

explanation: Right eigenvectors of an asymmetric matrix are generally not orthogonal, so \(V^\mathrm{T}V\ne I\). The correct transform is \(\alpha =V^{-1}h\), equivalently using the associated left eigenvectors to read amplitudes. Use right eigenvectors of W. If \(Wv_{i}=\lambda _{i} v_{i}\), multiplication by W rescales pattern \(v_{i}\) by \(\lambda _{i}\) without rotating it. Put these eigenvectors in the columns of V. If they are linearly independent, \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\). Expand activity as \(h=V\alpha\), where \(\alpha _{i}\) is the amplitude of population pattern i. This basis change leaves the physical state unchanged, just as a two-dimensional displacement can be expressed in oblique rather than x-y coordinates.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Normalization fixes lengths, not angles between vectors.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Asymmetric matrices can be diagonalizable with independent eigenvectors; nonorthogonality is not dependence.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Distinct eigenvalues generally ensure independence, not orthogonality; the latter needs additional matrix structure.

conceptTags: Eigenvalues Control Timescale, Fixed Points, and Integration
stem: Why does changing \(\lambda\) from 0.98 to 0.999 create drift risk in addition to longer memory?

choices.text: Only decay time increases twentyfold while constant-input gain is unchanged, so any resulting drift must come exclusively from numerical roundoff.
Decay time and constant-input gain both grow twentyfold, so persistent biases cause larger shifts as memory becomes longer.
Any eigenvalue below one forces all sustained-input displacements to vanish.
Moving closer to one strengthens leak, so persistent low-frequency biases are removed more rapidly even though the network retains its initial state for longer.

explanation: The denominator \(1-\lambda\) shrinks from 0.02 to 0.001, multiplying timescale and constant-input gain by twenty. A tiny persistent bias, low-frequency noise, or connectivity error produces a much larger state displacement. This also separates fixed point from timescale. For constant transformed input Ĩ_i and \(\lambda _{i}\ne 1\), \(\alpha _{i}*=\widetilde I_{i}/(1-\lambda _{i})\). The same small denominator creates both long \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and high steady-state gain, so near-integration amplifies constant bias and parameter error. Memory is the benefit and drift the risk. Negative feedback, multiple timescales, and nonlinear bounds can manage that sensitivity.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Both quantities share the same denominator, so persistent bias is amplified too.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Stability means approaching the driven steady state, which need not be zero.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Feedback offsets more leak near one, slowing restoration and magnifying persistent bias.

conceptTags: In the Eigenbasis, Coupled Neuronal Dynamics Decompose into Independent Modes
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “In the Eigenbasis, Coupled Neuronal Dynamics Decompose into Independent Modes”?

choices.text: Each mode is one anatomical neuron, so diagonalization proves that the original network contains no recurrent connections.
Transforming activity while leaving input in neuron coordinates gives every mode the correct drive, because external inputs bypass the recurrent weight matrix and need no coordinate change.
For a diagonalizable matrix, the inverse basis transform separates activity into modes, transformed inputs drive them, and the original basis reconstructs neuronal activity.
Every positive eigenvalue produces growth regardless of intrinsic leak.

explanation: If recurrent matrix W is diagonalizable as \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\), activity \(h=V\alpha\) expresses a neuronal-space pattern in eigenmode amplitudes. After left multiplication by \(V^{-1}\), each \(\alpha _{i}\) independently obeys \(\tau \dot{\alpha }_i=-(1-\lambda _{i})\alpha _{i}+\widetilde I_{i}\). Thus \(\lambda _{i}\), rather than one neuron, sets decay, integration, or growth of that population pattern. A basis change is a mathematical coordinate transformation; a mode is not an anatomical neuron.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Modes are population-coordinate directions, not individual cells; decoupling coordinates does not remove connections.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Inputs require the same inverse basis transform to determine the drive to each mode.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The continuous-time equation includes leak; a positive real eigenvalue below one can still produce decay.

conceptTags: Symmetric two-neuron network: natural coordinates for coupled equations
stem: If \(I_{1}=1\) and \(I_{2}=-1\), which mode is driven directly?

choices.text: Only the difference mode is driven; the signed inputs cancel in the common projection.
Only the common mode is driven: equal input magnitudes give \(\beta _{+}=\sqrt 2\).
Neither mode is driven, because zero total input makes the whole input vector zero.
Both modes receive equal nonzero drive, because each neuron receives an input of unit magnitude.

explanation: \(\beta _{+}=(1-1)/\sqrt 2=0\) and \(\beta _{-}=(1-(-1))/\sqrt 2=\sqrt 2\), so only the difference mode is driven directly; the neurons tend to change in opposite directions. Consider \(W=[[0,w_{0}],[w_{0},0]]\) with rate equations \(\tau dh_{1}/dt=-h_{1}+w_{0}h_{2}+I_{1}\) and \(\tau dh_{2}/dt=-h_{2}+w_{0}h_{1}+I_{2}\). Zeros on the diagonal mean that this teaching example has no self-coupling, while equal off-diagonal entries make the reciprocal coupling symmetric. That symmetry suggests testing \(h_{1}=h_{2}\) and \(h_{1}=-h_{2}\): exchanging the neurons leaves the first pattern unchanged and changes only the sign of the second.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: The common projection uses signed inputs: \(\beta _{+}=(1+(-1))/\sqrt 2=0\). Taking absolute values changes the input vector.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Zero total input removes the common projection only. Opposite nonzero components still drive the difference direction.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Modes are joint directions of both neurons. Project the signed input vector onto each direction instead of assigning drive according to individual input magnitudes.

conceptTags: Coupling strength sets time constants, integration, and stability
stem: At \(w_{0}=-0.9\), which mode is slowest, and what is its time constant in units of \(\tau\)?

choices.text: The common mode is slowest at \(10\tau\); the difference mode has a time constant of about \(0.526\tau\).
The difference mode is slowest at \(10\tau\); the common mode has time constant \(\tau/1.9\).
Both modes have time constant \(10\tau\), since both use the same coupling strength.
The difference time constant is \(-10\tau\), so this mode grows rather than decays.

explanation: The difference mode is slowest because \(\tau _{-}=\tau /(1-0.9)=10\tau\); the common mode has \(\tau _{+}=\tau /(1+0.9)\approx 0.526\tau\). Negative coupling near -1 preserves the opposing-change pattern. When \(|w_{0}|<1\), both 1-w0 and 1+w0 are positive, so both modes decay exponentially after input removal. As w0 approaches 1, \(\tau _{+}\) becomes long and the common coordinate behaves as a leaky integrator. At \(w_{0}=1\) the common equation has no leak: sustained input is integrated and the accumulated \(\alpha _{+}\) remains after the input ends. The same logic moves to the difference mode as w0 approaches -1. Equality marks a perfect integrator and should not be lumped into the ordinary leaky regime.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Negative coupling slows the difference direction. The common denominator is \(1-w_{0}=1.9\); the difference denominator is \(1+w_{0}=0.1\).
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: The modes have opposite coupling eigenvalues. Their time constants are \(\tau/(1-w_{0})\) and \(\tau/(1+w_{0})\), which are different here.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Here \(1+w_{0}=0.1>0\), giving a positive difference time constant. Both modes are stable when \(|w_{0}|<1\).

conceptTags: Activity-space and mode-space views of the same trajectory
stem: If a constant input \(\beta _{-}=1\) acts at every moment, must \(\alpha _{-}\) approach zero?

choices.text: Yes. Stability means every mode returns to the origin regardless of the sustained input.
Yes. A constant has zero derivative, so the input disappears from the first-order state equation.
No. With stable dynamics, sustained input shifts the difference mode to a nonzero fixed point.
No, but any constant difference input necessarily causes linear growth with no fixed point.

explanation: No. A stable difference mode approaches the nonzero fixed point \(\alpha _{-}* = \beta _{-}/(1+w_{0})\), so the trajectory can remain away from the common axis. Low-dimensional conclusions depend on input structure. Approximation quality can be measured by residual energy. Because the basis is orthonormal, \(||h||^{2}=\alpha +^{2}+\alpha -^{2}\). Discarding the difference mode gives squared reconstruction error exactly \(\alpha -^{2}\). An analyst may set a tolerance, for example calling the state 95% common-mode when \(\alpha -^{2}/(\alpha +^{2}+\alpha -^{2})<0.05\). This criterion is chosen for the analysis; it is not an absolute boundary that appears automatically in a sketch.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Stability describes convergence toward the input-dependent fixed point. Nonzero sustained difference input generally shifts that fixed point away from the origin.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: The equation contains the input itself, not its derivative. Constant drive remains in the steady-state balance.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: A stable difference mode retains a restoring term that can balance constant input. Linear growth under constant drive requires an integration mode with no restoring term.

conceptTags: PCA: from projection variance to covariance eigenvectors
stem: What is chiefly mixed in if \(E[hh^\mathrm{T}]\) is computed without centering?

choices.text: Nothing extra is included: taking an expectation automatically removes the mean, so a second moment always equals covariance.
Only a scalar multiple of the identity is added, so the eigenvectors must remain unchanged.
The recurrent matrix eigenvalues are included, automatically making the first PC the slowest dynamical mode.
The mean outer product can dominate the leading direction instead of fluctuations around the mean.

explanation: The mean outer-product term \(\bar{h}\) \(\bar{h}^\mathrm{T}\) is included, so the leading direction may represent the mean firing pattern rather than trial or temporal fluctuations. Modes of W and PCs of C align only under additional conditions. For example, in a linear network driven by isotropic noise at stationarity, with W normal or symmetric, slow dynamical modes often accumulate more variance. Structured input, unequal noise, trial conditions, and nonlinear observations can all rotate the covariance. Similar axes motivate a hypothesis; statistical collinearity does not identify recurrent weights by itself.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Expectation does not perform centering: \(E[hh^\mathrm{T}]=C+\bar{h}\bar{h}^\mathrm{T}\). Equality with covariance requires zero mean.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: The mean outer product is generally a directional rank-one term, not an isotropic identity term. It can rotate the leading direction.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: The extra term comes from the activity mean. Statistical covariance directions and recurrent dynamical modes need not coincide; inputs and noise also matter.

conceptTags: Top-K PCA, orthogonal projection, and the boundary between reversible and approximate representations
stem: Why does \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}=I\) not imply \(V_{K}V_{K}^\mathrm{T}=I\)?

choices.text: Column orthogonality gives a K-space identity; in N-space the product projects onto the retained subspace.
Orthogonal columns make \(V_{K}\) square, so reversing the multiplication order cannot change the identity.
\(V_{K}V_{K}^\mathrm{T}\) is the N-space identity because the transpose automatically reconstructs discarded coordinates.
Both products are simply \(K/N\) times an identity matrix and contain no directional information.

explanation: When \(K<N\), \(V_{K}\) is not square. \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}\) is the identity in K-space, while \(V_{K}V_{K}^\mathrm{T}\) is the N-space projector onto a K-dimensional subspace. Order the covariance eigenvalues \(\lambda _{1}\ge \lambda _{2}\ge \cdots \ge \lambda _{N}\) with orthonormal eigenvectors. The first component uses the direction of maximum variance. The second is orthogonal to it and maximizes variance in the remaining subspace. Continuing gives \(V_{K}=[v_{1},\cdots,vK]\), an N×K matrix. For one centered sample, score vector \(p=V_{K}^\mathrm{T}(h-\bar{h})\) has K coordinates.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: For \(K<N\), \(V_{K}\) has shape \(N\times K\). Column orthogonality does not supply the missing columns or make the matrix square.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Transposition maps retained coordinates back to activity space but cannot recover discarded components. Orthogonal-complement vectors map to zero, unlike an identity operator.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: An orthogonal projector preserves vectors in the retained subspace and removes vectors in its orthogonal complement. Its action is directional, not a uniform scalar rescaling.

conceptTags: Choosing dimensionality with the eigenvalue cliff and cumulative variance
stem: Why does '95% variance explained' not guarantee retention of 95% of behavioral information?

choices.text: It does guarantee this, because PCA ranks components by behavioral prediction accuracy.
Activity variance and behavioral information differ because the readout can use low-variance directions.
It does guarantee this, because the remaining 5% of variance must be measurement noise with no task information.
The only obstacle is that 95% variance means retaining 95% of neurons rather than all neurons.

explanation: Variance measures activity amplitude, whereas behavioral information depends on condition distributions and the decoder. A low-variance direction may reliably distinguish choices, so the two percentages are not generally equivalent. Cumulative variance explained \(F(K)=\sum _{k=1}^K\lambda _{k}/\sum _{j=1}^N\lambda _{j}\) increases monotonically from \(F(0)=0\) to \(F(N)=1\). Its numerator must be \(\sum _{j=1}^K\lambda _{j}\) and its denominator the total variance \(\sum _{j=1}^N\lambda _{j}\); writing only \(\lambda _{i}\) or omitting the denominator no longer represents cumulative explained variance. Thresholds of 80%, 90%, or 95% give reproducible rules but need not be optimal for a particular scientific question. Measurement noise can raise the tail, condition means can create large PCs, and trial averaging can change the spectrum. Report preprocessing and the selection criterion together with K.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: PCA ranks directions by activity variance without using behavioral labels. A high-variance direction may be behaviorally irrelevant, while a low-variance direction may carry a reliable signal.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: A variance fraction does not distinguish signal from noise. Behavioral readouts, conditional distributions, or held-out prediction are needed to assess retained behavioral information.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: PCA truncation retains population directions, not a percentage of neurons. Variance and behavioral information differ because they measure different statistical properties and depend on the readout.

conceptTags: Scree-plot cliff and cumulative variance
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Scree-plot cliff and cumulative variance”?

choices.text: After the cliff the eigenvalues decrease, so the cumulative variance curve must turn downward too.
The flat tail means all remaining PCs have exactly zero variance and can be removed without reconstruction error.
Individual eigenvalues fall after the cliff while cumulative variance keeps increasing toward 100%.
The cliff uniquely identifies the true neural dimensionality and guarantees preservation of all behavioral information.

explanation: Read the two curves in principal-component order: beyond the cliff, each eigenvalue contributes little additional variance, while cumulative variance continues to rise monotonically. The elbow suggests candidate dimensionalities but does not determine a unique cutoff; the plotted coordinates illustrate the normalized relation and are not empirical data.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Cumulative explained variance is a normalized partial sum of nonnegative eigenvalues. Smaller eigenvalues add less, but cannot subtract previously accumulated variance.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: A nearly flat tail means similar small eigenvalues, not necessarily zero eigenvalues. Removing directions with nonzero variance still creates reconstruction error.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: An elbow suggests candidate cutoffs. Noise, preprocessing, and analysis goals affect dimensionality selection, and retained activity variance does not guarantee retained behavioral information.

conceptTags: Sources of rhythm: pacemaker, follower, and network half-center
stem: If both cells stop alternating after the block but continue to oscillate at different frequencies, is this a purely network-generated rhythm?

choices.text: Yes. Loss of alternation proves that neither cell had any intrinsic oscillatory capacity before the block.
No. Coupling organizes alternation, but oscillations that persist after the block also indicate intrinsic rhythmic capacity.
Yes. Different frequencies merely reset the old network phase; every oscillation persisting after a complete block must still come from reciprocal inhibition.
Continued oscillation proves that both cells are merely followers of an external pacemaker and excludes any intrinsic contribution.

explanation: No. Coordinated alternation depends on network coupling, but each cell retains intrinsic oscillatory capacity; the full mechanism is coupled intrinsic oscillators. Distinguish two origins of rhythmic activity. A cell-intrinsic pacemaker continues to generate a rhythm from its own voltage-gated currents even without periodic synaptic input; a follower does not oscillate on its own and simply tracks synaptic drive from a pacemaker. A network-generated rhythm is different: individual cells may remain tonic or silent in isolation, but reciprocal inhibition makes the pair alternate activity as a half-center oscillator. Respiration and alternating muscles during walking are useful functional examples.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Alternation and individual oscillation are different observations. Continued oscillation after the block supports intrinsic rhythmic capacity.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: With a complete block, the removed reciprocal inhibition cannot still drive the rhythm. Separate frequencies are compatible with uncoupled intrinsic oscillators.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The observation does not identify an external pacemaker. Residual drive needs controls, but persistence does not exclude intrinsic oscillation.

conceptTags: Complex modes and damped oscillation in a linear two-neuron system
stem: What happens if the full eigenvalues are \(0.2\pm 5i s^{-1}\)?

choices.text: The trajectory spirals inward because the large imaginary part cancels the growth caused by the positive real part.
It immediately approaches a stable closed orbit: the imaginary part fixes frequency and the positive real part stabilizes a unique amplitude.
The trajectory spirals outward with an exponentially growing envelope; a bounded limit cycle would require nonlinear regulation.
The state grows monotonically without rotation, because any positive real part removes the dynamical effect of the imaginary part.

explanation: The trajectory rotates while its envelope grows as \(e^{0.2t}\), producing an outward spiral. The linear model is unstable; whether a limit cycle subsequently forms depends on nonlinear saturation. The characteristic polynomial \(\det(W-\lambda I)=\lambda ^{2}+w_{0}^{2}=0\) gives λ_W=±i|w0|. A complex-mode solution contains \(e^{(-1\pm iw0)t/\tau }=e^{-t/\tau }[\cos(|w_{0}|t/\tau )\pm i \sin(|w_{0}|t/\tau )]\). Combining the conjugate pair yields real sine–cosine trajectories for h1 and h2. The angular frequency is \(\omega =|w_{0}|/\tau \mathrm{rad}/s\), and the ordinary frequency is \(f=\omega /(2\pi )\).

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: The real part controls the envelope and the imaginary part the rotation rate; a large imaginary part does not cancel positive growth.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: A positive real part amplifies the linear solution without stabilizing amplitude. A stable cycle requires additional nonlinear structure.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The imaginary part still produces rotation. The positive real part changes the amplitude envelope during that rotation.

conceptTags: Morris–Lecar current balance, nullclines, and fixed points
stem: Why is a nullcline not the neuron's actual trajectory?

choices.text: A nullcline is already the trajectory; connecting its points in horizontal-coordinate order reveals the actual time course.
Every nullcline point stops both variables, so a trajectory remains there permanently as soon as it reaches either curve.
Only noise prevents a nullcline from being a trajectory; without noise every initial state follows the same nullcline.
A nullcline zeros one derivative, while the other variable may still change; only a joint intersection can be stationary.

explanation: A nullcline is only the set of points where one derivative is instantaneously zero. The other variable usually continues to change, so the state crosses or moves nearby; only an intersection of both nullclines can remain stationary. Read a phase plane by determining signs in each region. Whether \(dV/dt\) is positive on a given side of the V-nullcline must be checked with a test point, not guessed from the curve's appearance. Below the N-nullcline, usually \(N<N_{\infty }\) and arrows point upward; above it, arrows point downward. A fixed point is stable if nearby arrows converge, a saddle if one direction converges and another diverges, and unstable if the flow departs overall.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Geometric ordering is not temporal ordering. The vector field formed by both derivatives determines trajectory direction.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: One nullcline constrains only one derivative. A nonzero derivative of the other variable still moves the state.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Even a deterministic two-dimensional system can cross a nullcline because the other derivative is nonzero; noise is not required.

conceptTags: Relaxation cycles and phase geometry of a reciprocally inhibitory half-center
stem: Why can two mutually inhibitory cells generate a network rhythm even when neither oscillates in isolation?

choices.text: Inhibition switches the effective nullclines, and slow recovery can bring the partners to alternating transitions under suitable parameters.
Reciprocal inhibition creates a rhythm simply by fixing both voltages low; whether recovery changes over time is irrelevant.
Each inhibitory event permanently increases the partner’s input current; unbounded accumulation guarantees a stable cycle at every inhibitory strength.
Connecting the cells automatically eliminates their resting solutions, because any negative coupling makes every equilibrium unstable.

explanation: Inhibition switches each partner's effective nullcline between active and inactive conditions. Slow recovery makes the cells reach their transitions in turn, so coupling creates periodic state switching. Even if the fixed point of each isolated cell is stable, mutual inhibition plus recovery can make the pair oscillate; conversely, not every mutually inhibitory pair oscillates. The system needs an intrinsic variable that evolves slowly in active and inhibited phases, a suitable synaptic threshold, and the right ordering of transitions. A sensory pulse can push one cell across a separatrix and reset phase without generating the rhythm itself.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Two stationary low states are not an alternating rhythm. A mechanism must carry the system toward successive transitions.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Inhibition is not permanent accumulation of positive current. Rhythm depends on recovery, thresholds, and transition ordering, not arbitrary parameters.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: A negative weight alone does not remove or destabilize every fixed point. The coupled nullclines and vector field must be analyzed.

conceptTags: Intrinsic release and intrinsic escape: what triggers the phase switch?
stem: If the active cell falls below VT and its partner jumps 20 ms later, does that delay refute release?

choices.text: Yes. Release requires both voltage jumps at exactly the same instant, so any nonzero delay necessarily identifies escape.
No. Removal of inhibition can trigger the transition even though the partner takes finite time to leave its low state.
Yes. Firing after inhibition ends proves the inhibited cell had already escaped first, making the active cell’s fall a consequence.
No, but only if the delay is entirely a recording artifact and the released cell has no intrinsic transition dynamics.

explanation: No. Release requires only that removal of inhibition be the upstream trigger. The partner still takes finite time to leave its low state according to its own membrane and recovery dynamics. Approximate the synapse with a sharp threshold: \(S_{\infty }(V)=0\) when \(V<VT\) and 1 when \(V>VT\). While the active cell's V exceeds VT, it inhibits its partner; once V falls below VT, inhibition shuts off rapidly. A free neuron follows the \(F(V,N)=0\) nullcline, whereas an inhibited neuron follows a shifted nullcline that includes synaptic current. Switching between these two geometries makes the identity of the first threshold-crosser an observable mechanistic criterion.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Release specifies the causal trigger, not simultaneous completion of two finite-rate transitions.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: That reversed causal claim is not supported by the stated order. Diagnosing escape requires the state before inhibition is removed.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Membrane and recovery dynamics can themselves produce a delay; a measurement artifact is not necessary.

conceptTags: From a conductance oscillator to a rate–adaptation half-center
stem: Why are two linear rate variables h1 and h2 usually insufficient for a stable half-center limit cycle?

choices.text: Any imaginary eigenvalue automatically fixes a unique attracting amplitude, so adding a slow variable merely renames coordinates.
The only problem is neuron count: adding more fully linear units guarantees a unique stable limit cycle without nonlinear dynamics.
Linear rates lack attracting amplitude regulation; slow adaptation together with a nonlinearity can support bounded switching.
An arbitrary constant input is sufficient, because it automatically changes sign on each cycle to maintain alternation.

explanation: A linear system can only decay, rotate neutrally, or grow; it lacks a slow state and amplitude regulation. Adaptation or recovery plus nonlinear F supplies phase switching and a bounded cycle. While cell i is active, high \(h_{i}\) slowly raises \(a_{i}\). Increasing adaptation lowers effective drive until the active rate falls. Inhibition of the partner then weakens, allowing it to rise and subsequently inhibit the original cell. This is release-like switching. If \(a_{j}\) falls during the inhibited cell's low-activity phase, restoring its effective excitability until it crosses threshold first, switching is escape-like.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Purely imaginary modes have initial-condition-dependent orbits, not an attracting cycle; negative or positive real parts cause decay or growth.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Extra linear dimensions do not create attraction to a finite nonzero amplitude. Linear modes still follow their growth or decay rates.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: A constant input does not reverse sign each cycle. It can shift a linear fixed point without creating phase switching.

conceptTags: Morris–Lecar nullclines and the relaxation cycle
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Morris–Lecar nullclines and the relaxation cycle”?

choices.text: The nullclines are successive segments of one actual trajectory, and their stable intersection forces every initial state around the loop.
