Nearly horizontal crossings keep voltage fixed while recovery jumps rapidly; the outer branches instead show voltage rising at a constant speed.
The loop is determined only by the initial state; both derivatives vanish everywhere on it, so circulation needs no fast or slow changes.
Slow recovery along outer branches alternates with fast voltage jumps near folds; the unstable intersection does not trap the trajectory.

explanation: The intersection of the two nullclines is a candidate equilibrium. Here it is unstable, so the trajectory moves slowly along the outer attracting branches of the V-nullcline and jumps rapidly to the other branch near each fold. Long portions of the loop represent slow recovery, whereas nearly horizontal crossings represent fast voltage transitions. The curves are a normalized schematic of the mechanisms.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Nullclines are sets where derivatives vanish, not successive time segments. The illustrated intersection is unstable and the loop surrounds it.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Voltage is on the horizontal axis. Near-horizontal crossings mainly change voltage, whereas branch segments reflect slow recovery rather than constant-speed voltage growth.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Zero values of both derivatives imply stationarity, not circulation. The cycle requires nonzero flow along its path.

conceptTags: Eye-velocity integration, persistent position, and the bilateral circuit
stem: If position returns to center after the velocity command with a time constant of 5 s, is this still an integrator?

choices.text: It is perfect integration because reaching any nonzero state is sufficient, regardless of whether the state later decays.
It cannot be integration at all: any finite drift time proves the network never accumulated the velocity command, even approximately over short intervals.
It is a leaky integrator: short observations may look persistent, but a longer delay reveals the finite drift time scale.
Five seconds is a fixed latency: the position remains exactly unchanged for that interval and then jumps instantly to center.

explanation: It is a leaky rather than perfect integrator. Behavior may appear persistent for periods shorter than 5 s, but a long delay reveals measurable drift. Moving the eye requires phasic motor drive to generate velocity and tonic drive to oppose orbital restoring forces and hold the new position. The course abstracts the distributed brainstem and cerebellar network as a neural integrator: its input is the eye-velocity command \(v(t)\), and its output state approximates \(x(t)=x(0)+\int v(t')dt'\). Ideally, x retains its latest value when v returns to zero; if the network leaks, position slowly drifts back toward center.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Perfect integration retains the state after input ends. Measurable decay indicates a remaining leak toward center.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Integration can be leaky. The state can accumulate input while older contributions decay with a finite time constant.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: A time constant sets the scale of continuous exponential decay, not a deadline followed by an abrupt jump.

conceptTags: General \(2\times 2\) weights, eigenvalue one, and a compensating family
stem: What happens if the same constraint gives \(\lambda _{2}=1.1\)?

choices.text: The whole network remains stable because an eigenvalue of one automatically projects all other modes onto the memory direction.
The transverse mode decays faster because larger connectivity eigenvalues strengthen the restoring force, returning every deviation to the memory axis.
Both modes immediately become oscillatory because a second eigenvalue above one necessarily creates an imaginary pair.
The integrating mode remains, but the transverse mode amplifies small errors, so the whole network is not a stable integrator.

explanation: The memory mode still has \(\lambda =1\), but the transverse mode's full growth rate is \((1.1-1)/\tau >0\). Any small error grows, so the full network is not a stable, usable integrator. Expanding gives \(\det(I-W)=(1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})-W_{12}W_{21}=0\). If \(W_{12}\ne 0\), solve \(W_{21}=(1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})/W_{12}\). Once three weights are chosen, the fourth compensates; increasing a self-weight can be offset by changing cross-coupling while preserving \(\lambda =1\). This is a many-to-one functional mapping: different parameter points share the same integrator eigenvalue.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Canceling leak in one mode does not eliminate other eigendirections. Transverse stability must be checked separately.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: The full growth rate subtracts the intrinsic leak from the connectivity eigenvalue. Exceeding one makes that rate positive.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: A real eigenvalue above one indicates growth along that direction; it does not create an imaginary part or make another mode oscillate.

conceptTags: Biological variability and reparameterizing a nonlinear circuit fit
stem: Why does fitting become linear after fixing the nonlinearities even though the neuron response itself remains nonlinear?

choices.text: The fixed nonlinearities transform known data; unknown weights then combine those features linearly without linearizing the whole response.
Fixing the nonlinearities means replacing every activation function with the identity and discarding all thresholds and saturation.
All parameters of any nonlinear network can be fitted linearly; enough recordings automatically separate unknown activation curves from unique weights.
The fit necessarily uses a first-order Taylor expansion at one stimulus and is valid only for infinitesimal changes around it.

explanation: \(S_{j}\) and \(F_{i}^{-1}\) already apply nonlinear transformations to the data. Only the unknown weights linearly combine those transformed features; the full input–output mapping remains nonlinear. With the nonlinear functions fixed, the prediction is \(\hat{Y}_{i\mu }=\sum _j W_{ij} X_{j}\mu\), linear in the unknown weights Wij and bias. Each output neuron i can fit one row of weights independently. If M sample positions are columns, X has shape D×M, Y is N×M, W is N×D, and \(\hat{Y}=WX\) is dimensionally consistent. State this orientation explicitly, because placing samples in rows yields a transposed formula.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Fixed means known, not removed. Inverse response and synaptic transformations still enter the features and targets.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: The linear weight problem requires the relevant nonlinearities to be fixed and usable in the transformation. Identifiability still requires separate checks.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Here linearity concerns how weights enter, not necessarily a local Taylor approximation. Known nonlinear transformations can be evaluated directly.

conceptTags: Least squares, the closed-form solution, and the Hessian
stem: How does adding a ridge penalty \(\lambda ||w||^{2}/2\) change the Hessian?

choices.text: Ridge decreases Hessian eigenvalues, making flat directions flatter and thereby stabilizing the inverse.
Ridge adds a scaled identity to the Hessian, shifting its eigenvalues upward without supplying new observations.
The Hessian is unchanged: the penalty only shifts observed targets and cannot affect curvature, parameter bias, or numerical conditioning.
The penalty is equivalent to collecting independent neural observations; larger eigenvalues prove new experimental evidence for each parameter.

explanation: H becomes \(XX^\mathrm{T}+\lambda I\). Every eigenvalue increases by \(\lambda\), stabilizing the inverse, but the estimate is biased toward zero; regularization must not be mistaken for additional data. This connects fitting with experimental design. If one feature combination barely changes across positions, X contains little information along that direction and H has a small eigenvalue. Conditions that selectively activate that combination can increase curvature and tighten parameter uncertainty. Sloppiness need not be accepted passively; perturbations and improved sampling can reduce it.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: A positive quadratic penalty adds positive curvature rather than subtracting it, moving small eigenvalues away from zero.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: A quadratic penalty on weights directly contributes second derivatives and shrinks the estimate toward zero.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The extra curvature comes from the chosen penalty, not new measurements; regularization is not additional experimental evidence.

conceptTags: The Hessian eigenbasis, stiff/sloppy directions, and model ensembles
stem: Why can sloppy not be translated as 'this parameter is unimportant'?

choices.text: A sloppy eigenvector must contain only one synapse, which can therefore be deleted without changing any model prediction.
Low curvature establishes irrelevance under every possible stimulus, behavior, and parameter scaling, eliminating the need for perturbation tests.
Sloppiness is low curvature of a parameter combination under this loss; that direction may still affect unmeasured behavior.
Sloppiness necessarily means more neural noise, because parameter-Hessian eigenvalues are the eigenvalues of activity covariance.

explanation: A Hessian direction usually combines parameters, and small curvature means only that the current data and loss are insensitive to it. The combination may still be crucial for an unmeasured behavior, a perturbation response, or biological viability. A Hessian is symmetric positive-semidefinite, so \(H=VDV^\mathrm{T}\), where columns \(v_{k}\) are orthonormal parameter directions and D contains \(\lambda _{k}\ge 0\). Let \(z=V^\mathrm{T}(w-\hat{w})\); then the quadratic loss increase is \(\Delta L=1/2\sum \lambda _{k} z_{k}^{2}\). A large \(\lambda _{k}\) gives a large loss for the same displacement and defines a stiff direction. A small \(\lambda _{k}\) permits farther movement within the adequate-fit contour and defines a sloppy direction.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: A Hessian direction usually combines parameters. Insensitivity in current data does not establish invariance of every prediction.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Curvature depends on data, loss, and parameter scaling. New conditions can constrain a previously sloppy combination.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Loss curvature in parameter space and covariance in neural activity space are different objects and cannot be equated.

conceptTags: Three fates of an eigenvalue-one integrator
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Three fates of an eigenvalue-one integrator”?

choices.text: The curves differ only in initial amplitude; once input ends, every mode of a linear network must decay with the same time constant.
An eigenvalue above one produces stronger restoring force, so the growing curve should decay fastest and only values below one amplify errors.
The persistent middle curve proves stability of the entire network under every perturbation, eliminating any need to check other eigenvalues or transverse modes.
After input ends, the mode decays, persists, or grows according to its eigenvalue; one integrating mode does not stabilize every other direction.

explanation: After input is removed, the fate of the same initial mode amplitude depends only on \(1-\lambda\): when \(\lambda <1\) it leaks; when \(\lambda =1\) the restoring coefficient in the derivative vanishes and memory persists; when \(\lambda >1\) a small deviation grows. Thus \(\det(I-W)=0\) guarantees only an integrating mode, and the stability of all remaining modes must still be checked.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: The connectivity eigenvalue relative to leak differs across the curves, changing growth rates; initial amplitude is not the sole difference.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: This reverses the sign: above one, recurrent feedback exceeds leak and the full mode has a positive growth rate.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Persistence of one mode only establishes absence of leak in that direction; other directions can still decay or grow.

conceptTags: Center-out tuning and low-dimensional population trajectories
stem: Why does a PC explaining 70% of neural variance not necessarily explain 70% of behavioral variance?

choices.text: Because PCA ranks neural directions using behavioral labels, the percentages agree exactly whenever those labels are noise free.
The only issue is neuron count: recording every cell makes every linear readout preserve variance fractions, forcing both percentages to be 70%.
Seventy percent neural variance means the PC contains seventy percent of cells, while behavioral variance counts the remainder.
Behavior depends on its readout: a high-variance neural direction may be ignored while a low-variance direction strongly affects output.

explanation: Behavior depends on a separate readout map, which may ignore high-variance directions or amplify low-variance directions; there is no fixed ratio between the two variances. A center-out task begins at a central location and reaches toward multiple radial targets, making direction, speed, and time from the go cue well structured. For one neuron, mean directional tuning can be described by \(r(\theta )=b+k \cos(\theta -\theta _{\mathrm{pref}})\), where \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}\) is preferred direction and k is modulation depth. This formula summarizes a condition average; it does not mean the neuron 'knows' the angle or guarantee that other movement variables have been excluded.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: PCA ranks neural variance without using behavioral labels. Noise-free labels do not equate the two variance fractions.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Even with complete observations, a readout can select or weight directions differently and change the composition of output variance.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: A principal component is a direction in recorded activity coordinates; explained variance is not a fraction of neurons.

conceptTags: Latent space, activity space, and the GPFA observation model
stem: If one latent factor is multiplied everywhere by 2 without changing C, is it still the same GPFA model?

choices.text: No. With the loading fixed, the predicted mean changes; observational equivalence requires inverse scaling of that loading column.
It is unchanged because latent factors are unobserved, so arbitrarily rescaling them cannot affect the observation distribution.
It remains equivalent if residual covariance doubles, since extra zero-mean noise exactly cancels the doubled factor contribution to the mean.
The corresponding loading column should also double, because scaling both factors in the same direction preserves their product and the mean.

explanation: No; the predicted mean changes. It is an equivalent coordinate reparameterization only if the corresponding column of C is also divided by 2. A K-dimensional trajectory in latent space is embedded by C into N-dimensional activity space. The column span of C is the shared-activity subspace allowed by the model, while \(\Sigma\) usually absorbs neuron-specific residuals. Shared variation does not require neuron pairs to have identical waveforms: positive and negative loadings allow one factor to produce different amplitudes and directions across cells.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Unobserved does not mean causally absent from the model. The factor enters the observation mean through its loading.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Residual covariance controls variability around the mean; it cannot cancel a systematic change in the predicted mean.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Doubling both factors multiplies their product by four. Preserving the observation product requires inverse scaling.

conceptTags: GP temporal kernels, parameter fitting, and delayed-reach trajectories
stem: Why does a smooth kernel not prove that the true cortical trajectory is intrinsically smooth?

choices.text: The kernel only decorates the plot; it does not affect latent inference, so all apparent smoothness comes from data.
Smoothness partly comes from the prior, so held-out data, alternative kernels, and temporal resolution must test its support.
A differentiable kernel proves identical differentiability in the real population, regardless of sample size or whether observations are held out.
The smooth kernel removes all observation noise, so lower training reconstruction error alone rules out oversmoothing or an incorrect time scale.

explanation: Some smoothness comes from the prior. Compare held-out data, alternative kernels, and temporal resolutions to determine whether the data support that time scale. Read a delayed-reach plot along its timeline. The interval after target onset but before the go cue is the preparatory epoch; movement begins only after go. Preparatory activity for different targets may approach different latent locations without producing obvious movement. After the cue, trajectories depart from those initial states along target-specific movement paths. The plot supports the idea that an initial condition influences later dynamics, but trajectories alone cannot exclude sustained common input.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: The kernel specifies temporal covariance of latent states and therefore affects inference, not just plot appearance.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: A mathematical property of the model prior is not an established biological property; data must distinguish alternative temporal structures.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Smoothing does not guarantee the true trajectory. Training fit cannot replace held-out prediction and time-scale sensitivity checks.

conceptTags: Preparatory activity, linear readouts, and output-null space
stem: If the downstream readout changes to \(U'\), must the original output-null vector remain null?

choices.text: It must remain null because zero output means that every neuron in the original vector is silent.
It must remain null because neuron count alone determines the null directions, regardless of weight rotations or which muscles are read out.
No. Nullness is relative to a readout; the same activity direction can be silent for one output and potent for another.
It must become nonzero: changing any readout entry makes it impossible to share a nonzero null vector with the original matrix.

explanation: No. The null space depends on the particular readout. One neural direction may be irrelevant to one output yet affect another muscle group or cognitive variable. Output-null does not mean computation-null. Activity along a null direction can set a recurrent initial condition, suppress an erroneous movement, or prepare multiple candidates. The same neural vector may also affect unrecorded downstream populations. The course diagram is a linear framework that separates the existence of activity from the existence of current output; it does not justify calling null activity biologically functionless.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: A nonzero activity vector can cancel under a particular readout. Zero output does not imply a zero neural state.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Matrix size and rank constrain null-space dimension, but the actual null directions depend on the weights.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Two different readouts may share null directions. A weight change guarantees neither preservation nor loss of nullness for a given vector.

conceptTags: Closed-loop BMI and cross-day latent alignment
stem: Why can an improvement in closed-loop performance not be attributed entirely to more accurate decoder parameters?

choices.text: Feedback cannot change the participant’s fixed neural signal, so every improvement measures only decoder accuracy.
Online updates necessarily worsen the decoder, so improvement can only come from the participant and requires no controls even when both change.
Once latent trajectories align across days, every neuron and the participant’s entire strategy are proven fixed, removing the need to assess adaptation.
Feedback can change neural strategy while the decoder also adapts; separating their contributions requires controlling one side.

explanation: The participant changes neural strategy in response to feedback, and the decoder may update online. Performance comes from joint adaptation, so one side must be frozen or otherwise controlled to separate the causes. A BMI decoder maps neural features to cursor velocity, position, or a discrete action. During open-loop calibration, the participant observes prescribed movement or attempts an action while the system fits a mapping offline. In closed loop, decoder output immediately changes visual feedback, so participant and decoder coadapt. Closed-loop performance is therefore not a passive measure of a fixed encoding; the brain, decoder, and feedback form a new dynamical system.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Closed-loop output becomes new input to the participant, who can learn and adjust; the neural distribution need not remain fixed.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Online updates can help or harm performance. A single outcome measure cannot uniquely assign contributions when both sides change.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Latent alignment does not require fixed individual-cell loadings or strategy and does not rule out closed-loop learning.

conceptTags: From population activity to closed-loop BMI
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “From population activity to closed-loop BMI”?

choices.text: Daily latent coordinates are aligned before shared decoding, and cursor feedback returns to affect subsequent neural activity.
Alignment merely overlays plots after feedback and never changes the coordinates given to the shared decoder.
A shared decoder rules out participant adaptation; the feedback arrow merely displays output and later activity must retain the open-loop calibration distribution.
A transferable cross-day map requires every neuron’s loading to remain permanently fixed; changing one loading makes stable latent decoding impossible.

explanation: Observed activity is first compressed by GPFA into daily latent coordinates, then \(A_{d}\) aligns those coordinates to a shared space and passes them to shared decoder B. Decoder output changes cursor feedback, which in turn changes subsequent neural activity. Cross-day stability therefore means that a low-dimensional mapping is transferable; it does not require each neuron's loading to remain fixed.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: The alignment map sits between latent inference and the shared decoder and therefore changes the decoder’s input coordinates.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Feedback can alter strategy and neural distributions. Shared parameters do not make the closed-loop system passive or open loop.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Population structure can remain alignable despite individual loading changes; stable latent decoding does not require fixed single-cell identity.

conceptTags: A working definition of cognition: internal state beyond current input
stem: Why does continued brain activity with the eyes closed not by itself prove cognition in this lecture's sense?

choices.text: Persistent activity may reflect spontaneous fluctuation or unmeasured input; its link to task history and later behavior remains unproven.
Closing the eyes eliminates all external and bodily input, making every remaining fluctuation an exact working memory of prior events.
The definition only requires ongoing firing, with no relation to history, goals, or behavior, so any nonzero mean firing rate is sufficient.
The sole obstacle is that cognition requires complete neural silence; any active internal state would be destroyed by being represented.

explanation: Persistent activity may be spontaneous fluctuation or an unmeasured input. It must carry task-relevant history and predict later behavior. This lecture adopts a working definition: cognition makes brain state or behavior incompletely determined by present sensory input. The same current stimulus can produce different responses under different memories, goals, or beliefs; conversely, an internal decision variable can keep evolving while the outside world is unchanged. This definition is useful for modeling, but it is not a complete philosophical definition of consciousness, language, or intelligence.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Closing the eyes leaves other sensory inputs, bodily state, and spontaneous activity. Persistence does not identify information content.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: The working definition concerns dependence beyond current input, requiring tests of relevant history rather than mere activity.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The definition does not require silence. Historical and task relevance matter; activity or silence alone is insufficient.

conceptTags: Timelines of DMS and Romo parametric working memory
stem: Why does monotonic delay-period firing with f1 not by itself prove that this is the memory used for behavior?

choices.text: Monotonic tuning guarantees this is the sole memory source, because no other neurons can represent the same ordering of stimuli.
The signal may be a passive readout; trial variability, selective perturbations, or downstream coupling must link it to comparison behavior.
A sufficiently long delay average turns correlation into causation, even if perturbing the signal leaves comparison behavior entirely unchanged.
It cannot be memory because every monotonic code can only represent a motor command, never an earlier stimulus frequency.

explanation: The correlated signal could be a passive readout. Functional evidence is stronger when its trial fluctuations, selective perturbation, or downstream coupling affect comparison behavior. In the Romo vibration task, frequency f1 is delivered to a fingertip, followed after a delay by f2; the animal judges whether f2 is greater or less than f1. Comparing neighboring frequencies requires a graded magnitude, not merely a 'stimulus occurred' marker. If the delay representation is noisy, f1 and f2 become harder to discriminate as they approach each other, and psychometric slope can estimate their combined sensory and memory uncertainty.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Several populations can encode the same stimulus correlatively. Monotonicity does not exclude copies or common drive.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Longer averaging does not establish functional causality; perturbations, trial predictions, and downstream use need independent evidence.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Monotonic coding can represent frequency or other variables. The unresolved issue is behavioral use, not the code’s monotonic form.

conceptTags: Persistent activity and a recurrent mode near one
stem: Why does increasing \(\lambda\) from 0.99 to 1.01 not simply lengthen memory a little?

choices.text: Larger eigenvalues always stabilize the mode, so crossing one merely increases the decay time slightly.
The mode automatically forms a stable closed orbit; crossing one supplies both frequency and saturated amplitude without any further nonlinearity.
The change crosses the stability boundary, turning slow decay into exponential growth that needs nonlinear amplitude control.
The mode stops responding to input because recurrent feedback above one exactly cancels every external drive and leaves only zero activity.

explanation: It crosses the stability boundary. The linear mode changes from slow decay to exponential growth and needs another nonlinearity to limit amplitude. Persistent activity of individual neurons may change over time while a population projection remains stable. Conversely, a condition-averaged cell may look flat because different trial dynamics cancel. Examine decoding across the delay, population trajectories, single-trial drift, and behavioral error together. Short-term memory need not alter synaptic weights online on every trial; the existing recurrent network state can store it.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: The full growth rate passes through zero at one and becomes positive above it; it is no longer a decay time.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Instability of a real mode does not automatically supply an oscillation frequency or saturation; the full nonlinear system must be examined.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Exceeding one makes the homogeneous component grow; it does not cancel arbitrary input and instead amplifies small deviations.

conceptTags: Leaky drift-diffusion: evidence, noise, and first passage
stem: Why do identical coherence values yield different choices and RTs?

choices.text: Equal coherence fixes every evidence sample, so different choices must be assigned randomly after accumulation rather than arise from model noise.
Both boundaries encode the same choice; their signs distinguish fast from slow responses.
Different response times require different coherences, because repeating a stochastic process with fixed parameters necessarily repeats its exact path.
Equal coherence fixes mean evidence, not each noise path; the first boundary reached and its crossing time can therefore vary.

explanation: Each trial has a different noise path, which changes both the first-passage time and which boundary is reached first. In simulation, update a with a small step \(\Delta t\) and stop at the first boundary crossing; do not average after crossing and then decide. Noise scaling must vary with the square root of \(\Delta t\). Adding a fixed-variance noise term each step makes the model change when the time step changes. Begin with deterministic constant evidence, then add randomness and observe how the distribution forms.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Coherence does not fix each stochastic realization. Accumulated noise itself changes the first-passage direction and timing.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: The first boundary identifies the choice, and its crossing time is a modeled decision variable, not a plotting artifact.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Fixed distribution parameters do not fix a random sample; identical parameters permit different noise paths.

conceptTags: Psychometric and chronometric functions and LIP ramping
stem: Why can mean LIP ramp slopes alone not distinguish accumulation from averaged discrete steps?

choices.text: Variable step times can average into a smooth ramp, so mean slopes alone require follow-up comparison of single-trial models.
Trial averaging preserves every sharp step, so a smooth mean excludes all discrete-switching models at the single-trial level.
The two models necessarily have opposite mean slopes, so slope sign alone identifies the mechanism without trial distributions, timing, or choice conditioning.
Sampling the same mean curve more densely uniquely recovers whether each individual trial contained a discrete step.

explanation: Both forms of single-trial dynamics can yield similar smooth curves when different onset or choice times are averaged, requiring single-trial model comparison. A psychometric function plots P(choice|signed coherence). Choice is nearly uncertain around zero coherence and saturates toward the correct option as coherence magnitude grows. Horizontal displacement suggests bias, while slope reflects overall sensitivity but also depends on sensory noise, integration, and lapses. An accuracy curve alone often cannot distinguish drift, bound, and noise.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Steps at different trial times can average into a gradual curve. A smooth mean does not guarantee smooth individual trials.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Both single-trial processes can produce mean ramps in the same direction. Slope sign has no unique mapping to mechanism.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Denser sampling of an average cannot recover information lost by averaging across trials; individual recordings and model comparisons are needed.

conceptTags: Wong–Wang choice attractors and phase-plane boundaries
stem: Why do two choice attractors generally require a saddle or basin boundary between them?

choices.text: The basins can overlap, so one deterministic initial state converges simultaneously to both choices.
Distinct attraction basins require a separating boundary, often the stable manifold of a saddle in a planar choice model.
Every nullcline is automatically an uncrossable basin boundary, so all decision boundaries follow without analyzing trajectories, saddles, or the vector field.
The boundary must itself be a third stable choice attractor that draws nearby states into an additional behavioral option.

explanation: Distinct basins of attraction in a continuous dynamical system must be separated by a boundary that flows to neither attractor. In two dimensions, that boundary is commonly the stable manifold of a saddle. Intersections of \(G_{1}=0\) and \(G_{2}=0\) are fixed points. Under absent or weak evidence, a common topology contains a low-activity undecided state, two choice attractors, and a saddle on the basin boundary. Other parameter settings produce other topologies, so the schematic is not a universal theorem. A separatrix through the saddle assigns initial states and noise paths to the two attractor basins.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: A deterministic initial state has one trajectory and cannot simultaneously converge to two distinct attractors.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: A nullcline zeros only one derivative and can generally be crossed; basin boundaries follow from the full dynamics.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: A saddle’s stable manifold can separate basins without the saddle being a third stable choice attracting a full neighborhood.

conceptTags: First-passage paths in drift–diffusion
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “First-passage paths in drift–diffusion”?

choices.text: Choice is determined by final average height; after the first crossing, continue accumulating and classify the trial using the average of both paths.
The positive boundary means a slow response and the negative boundary a fast response of the same choice, while horizontal position represents stimulus strength.
With the same parameters, noise can reach opposite boundaries; first-crossing sign gives choice and crossing time gives decision time.
Opposite boundaries prove different mean evidence; at fixed coherence, noise can change timing but never the direction of choice.

explanation: Each path begins at bias b, accumulates noisy evidence step by step, and stops the first time it reaches +B or −B. The endpoint determines choice and the horizontal coordinate determines decision time. Under identical task parameters, noise can carry the two trajectories to different boundaries; a trajectory must not be averaged further after crossing before a decision is assigned.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: A first-passage decision ends at the initial crossing; later samples or averages over other trials cannot redefine that decision.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Boundary sign identifies the two choices, and time is read on the horizontal axis; this interpretation swaps their meanings.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Fixed mean evidence does not fix the noise path. Stochastic accumulation can change both timing and the first boundary reached.

conceptTags: Learned choice and three-factor synaptic credit
stem: Why should a dopamine pulse without preceding eligibility not selectively strengthen one stimulus–action synapse?

choices.text: The dopamine pulse itself contains each synapse's address, so a local activity record is unnecessary.
Dopamine broadcasts the outcome, while local eligibility identifies participating synapses; without it, selective credit has no address.
A rewarded action should strengthen every stimulus-action synapse equally, including those inactive during selection, to store the whole action.
Eligibility supplies the reward's sign, whereas dopamine specifies the individual synapse to update.

explanation: The third factor broadcasts the outcome, but local eligibility identifies the synapse that participated in the action; without eligibility, there is no correct credit address. A foraging animal selects an action from a sensory cue and receives reward. Learning must establish the stimulus–action–outcome relation rather than strengthen every recently active synapse. Let x be a presynaptic stimulus feature and y postsynaptic or action activity, so xy creates eligibility. A third factor M arrives after the outcome, giving update \(\Delta w=\eta Mxy\). An eligibility trace can bridge the delay from action to reward.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: A broadcast third factor does not identify which synapses participated in the preceding action.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Equal strengthening assigns credit to inactive synapses and loses the required local specificity.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: These roles are reversed: eligibility marks local participation and the third factor carries the outcome signal.

conceptTags: Reward baseline, covariance rule, and equilibrium
stem: Why does an underestimated baseline produce systematic positive drift?

choices.text: Lowering the baseline increases reward variance, so positive drift must occur even when eligibility has zero mean.
The baseline changes update noise only and can never affect the mean weight update.
A low baseline leaves a positive mean reward difference; positive mean eligibility then adds an update unrelated to covariance.
A lower baseline makes the mean reward difference more negative and therefore suppresses all action weights until choices cease.

explanation: The mean of R-b becomes positive. If mean eligibility is also positive, an offset update appears that is unrelated to genuine reward–eligibility covariance. A baseline may be a global running average or depend on state or choice. A global baseline has lower variance but can be biased when reward scales differ across states. A state-dependent value baseline is more precise but requires additional parameters. For its expected conditional dependence to remain valid, the baseline must not improperly inspect the outcome of the current action.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Subtracting a constant leaves variance unchanged; the extra drift depends on mean eligibility.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: A baseline error multiplied by nonzero mean eligibility changes the expected update.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The baseline is subtracted from reward, so lowering it increases rather than decreases the difference.

conceptTags: Matching law and choice allocation in fly foraging
stem: Why does a matching curve not prove that the animal explicitly computes RA/RB?

choices.text: Matching can occur only after neurons explicitly divide the total rewards obtained from the two options.
The matching ratio is fixed entirely by the experimenter's nominal reward probabilities and cannot depend on obtained rewards or choice history.
Enough repeated choices make the matching curve identify a unique synaptic update rule.
Local updates and stochastic choices can produce matching over time; the behavioral ratio alone does not identify the internal computation.

explanation: A long-run ratio can emerge automatically from local prediction-error updates and stochastic choice; the behavioral equality does not uniquely identify the internal algorithm. The derivation assumes continued sampling of both sides, an approximately stationary reward schedule, comparable cost per choice, and negligible changeover delay, satiety, and risk sensitivity. When reward magnitudes differ, match obtained value rather than raw count. Undermatching, overmatching, and bias can be described by generalized matching: \(\log(CA/CB)=a \log(RA/RB)+\log b\).

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Local learning and stochastic choice can also generate the same long-run allocation.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Matching concerns obtained reward allocation, which depends jointly on the schedule and choices.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: More repetitions improve precision without necessarily distinguishing algorithms with the same behavioral prediction.

conceptTags: Rescorla–Wagner, blocking, and the temporal-difference bridge
stem: If reward is unchanged but the prediction from old cue A is removed, why does B begin learning again?

choices.text: Removing A's prediction lowers the total prediction, restoring a positive error that updates B when B is active.
An unchanged reward guarantees an unchanged prediction error, so B cannot learn further.
Removing A creates a larger negative error, so B must first lose value before it can learn the unchanged reward.
B automatically copies all of A's removed weights without being active or receiving further feedback.

explanation: The total prediction falls and positive prediction error returns. Because B is active, it now receives an update—the logic of unblocking. Rescorla–Wagner and TD both depend on feature representation. Blocking changes if A and B are highly similar or a hidden context shifts; zero error may also reflect reduced attention. A model account should state alternative mechanisms and distinguish them with unblocking, reward revaluation, and trial-level learning curves.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Prediction error depends on reward minus the total prediction, not reward alone.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Lowering the total prediction while holding reward fixed shifts the error in the positive direction.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The update combines the active feature with current prediction error; it does not transfer weights directly.

conceptTags: Temporal features, state–action value, and choice
stem: Why does equal state value not imply that two actions are equally good?

choices.text: All actions in a state must have equal values, or the state's value cannot be defined.
State value averages action values under the policy; knowing that average does not establish equality among the individual actions.
State value equals only the most frequently selected action's value and ignores every other action even when its probability is positive.
Equal immediate rewards guarantee equal action values regardless of later transitions and policies.

explanation: V is a policy-weighted average. One action may have high Q and another low Q while producing the same aggregate V under a particular policy. In a delayed task, expand a sustained cue into time-specific features x1,x2,… so the learner knows which interval follows the cue. TD updates begin with features near reward and propagate to earlier features across trials. One time-invariant feature cannot easily represent when reward will arrive or predict a negative error at omission time.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: State value is well defined as a policy-weighted average of unequal action values.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Every action with positive policy probability contributes to the expected state value.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Action values also include future rewards, which can differ after identical immediate rewards.

conceptTags: Dopamine RPE timelines and the boundary with action selection
stem: Why does an omission dip support prediction error more strongly than merely observing no burst at reward time?

choices.text: Receiving no reward necessarily stops all neural activity, so the omission response adds no information.
No burst at predicted reward already proves prediction error uniquely, so the additional timed negative omission response places no further constraint on a model.
Omission produces a below-baseline signal at the expected time, adding a timed negative error that a nonnegative reward detector cannot readily explain.
The dip merely detects a physically negative reward and does not depend on prior expectation.

explanation: It is a negative signal below baseline timed to the expected reward. A purely nonnegative reward detector cannot naturally generate this timed negative response. If predicted reward is omitted at its expected time, \(Rt+1=0\) and next value collapses, making \(\delta\) negative at that moment and producing a dip. Accurate dip timing requires a temporal representation of when reward should arrive; a one-state-per-trial model cannot place the negative error precisely. Together, the three timelines constrain a prediction-error account rather than a pure reward response.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: The relevant observation is a timed decline relative to baseline, not cessation of all activity.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Other mechanisms could suppress a burst; a timed negative response imposes an additional constraint.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: An omitted expected reward can produce a negative error without any negative physical stimulus.

conceptTags: TD error transfers from reward to a predictive cue
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “TD error transfers from reward to a predictive cue”?

choices.text: After learning, the cue and the predicted reward retain equally large positive errors because each is independently counted as a new reward.
Omission merely removes a positive response and never produces a below-baseline dip.
The omission dip precedes the cue, so learning the interval between cue and reward is unnecessary for generating the illustrated response.
Learning shifts positive error to the cue; expected reward gives little error, while omission gives negative error at the expected time.

explanation: Compare the same trial row by row. Before learning, only unexpected reward produces positive \(\delta\). After the cue–reward relation is learned, positive \(\delta\) moves earlier to the cue and is nearly zero when reward arrives on time. If reward is omitted at the deadline, negative \(\delta\) appears then. This pattern of signs supports prediction error rather than a pure reward response.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: An already predicted reward no longer carries the same positive surprise.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: The figure explicitly shows a negative error at the expected reward time.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: The dip occurs at the predicted reward deadline, which requires temporal prediction.

conceptTags: MDPs and Markov states: compressing history into a predictive state
stem: Why might adding the trial number to state improve training prediction but still be a poor representation?

choices.text: Every extra variable guarantees a Markov state, making any training improvement sufficient proof of a correct representation.
A valid Markov state must retain the complete raw history without compressing it.
Trial IDs may memorize samples without capturing future-relevant structure, so predictions can fail in new contexts.
Random environmental transitions rule out any useful Markov state, leaving trial number as the only possible representation available to the learner.

explanation: It may memorize samples without capturing generalizable, future-relevant structure and will perform poorly in held-out contexts. An MDP is defined by states, actions, reward, and the transition–reward distribution \(p(s',r|s,a)\). The Markov property says that, conditioned on current s and a, the next outcome does not change with earlier trajectory. It does not require a deterministic environment: one s,a pair may lead randomly to several \(s'\) values, provided the probabilities are determined fully by current state.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Adding a variable need not capture all future-relevant information, and training error does not prove conditional independence.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Only information needed to predict the future must be retained, not every past observation.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Markov transitions may be stochastic; the condition concerns remaining dependence on history.

conceptTags: Discounted return, \(V_{\pi }\), and \(Q_{\pi }\)
stem: Why does a in \(Q_{\pi }(s,a)\) fix only the first step?

choices.text: Action value requires repeating that same action forever, regardless of later states.
After the fixed first action, every later action must maximize value even when the evaluated policy is explicitly exploratory or otherwise nongreedy.
Fixing the first action removes all environmental randomness, so no expectation over future outcomes is needed.
The action condition fixes the first move only; after reaching the next state, future actions follow the policy being evaluated.

explanation: The definition conditions on \(a_{t}=a\). Future actions are sampled from \(\pi\) beginning in the next state, so Q evaluates 'take a first, then follow \(\pi\).' \(V_{\pi }(s)=E_{\pi }[G_{t}|s_{t}=s]\) averages over environmental randomness and future policy actions. \(Q_{\pi }(s,a)=E_{\pi }[G_{t}|s_{t}=s,a_{t}=a]\) fixes only the first action, after which \(\pi\) is followed. Consequently, \(V_{\pi }(s)=\sum _{a}\pi (a|s)Q_{\pi }(s,a)\); under a deterministic policy, only the selected action contributes.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: The condition fixes the initial action rather than the entire future action sequence.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Policy action value follows the stated policy thereafter, not an automatically substituted optimal policy.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Transitions, rewards, and later actions can remain random after conditioning on the first action.

conceptTags: Bellman recursion: from the entire future to a one-step backup
stem: Why can the maximum not be moved outside the expectation while fixing the same \(a'\)?

choices.text: Different successor states may have different best actions; averaging first and fixing one action removes state-dependent continuation choices.
Maximum and expectation always commute because expectation is linear for every operation.
The next action must be fixed before the successor state is observed, or the current value violates the Markov condition and cannot be defined.
Moving the maximum outside permits independent optimal actions in each successor state and therefore increases flexibility.

explanation: Different random next states can have different best actions. Averaging first would force one action across states and change the optimal-continuation problem. The Bellman operator maps one Q table to another. In the tabular discounted setting with \(\gamma <1\) it is a contraction, so repeated backups approach a unique fixed point. As \(\gamma\) approaches 1, information reaches farther but contraction slows. Function approximation and off-policy sampling can invalidate this simple convergence guarantee.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Linearity of expectation does not allow an arbitrary nonlinear maximum to move outside it.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: A Markov policy can depend on the state actually reached; it need not use one action across states.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: An outer fixed action removes, rather than adds, state-dependent freedom.

conceptTags: Tabular Q-learning and exploration
stem: Why can the random branch of ε-greedy still select the greedy action?

choices.text: The random branch must exclude the greedy action to count as exploration.
The random branch samples all actions, including the greedy one, so it contributes additional probability to selecting that action.
The random branch weights actions in proportion to their values, so it always chooses the greedy action more often than any alternative.
Conditional on entering the random branch, greedy choice has probability epsilon divided by the number of actions, since branch-entry probability must be counted again.

explanation: The random branch samples uniformly from all actions, including the greedy action, so total greedy probability exceeds \(1-\epsilon\). In behavioral analysis, exploration should not simply be labeled random error; animals may direct exploration toward uncertain actions. Fitting ε-greedy to systematic uncertainty seeking misattributes it to value or temperature. Model comparisons should include alternatives such as softmax and directed exploration.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: The standard epsilon-greedy random branch samples uniformly from all actions.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: This branch is uniform rather than value weighted.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Given the random branch, each action has conditional probability one divided by the action count. Multiplying by epsilon gives this branch’s contribution to the unconditional probability.

conceptTags: Tolman mazes, latent state, and generative maps
stem: Why is immediate sensitivity to revaluation not sufficient proof of a complete internal map?

choices.text: Any immediate response to reward revaluation can arise only from a complete generative map.
One place-tuned hippocampal neuron proves that the animal explicitly stores every environmental transition and reward and uses this map for the decision.
Rules, instructions, or direct cues can also change choices rapidly; novel transitions and controls are needed to test map-based planning.
Immediate choice changes exclude every learning mechanism and reveal nothing about state representation.

explanation: Other rules, instructions, or direct cues can also alter choice rapidly; constrain the explanation with multiple novel transitions and control conditions. Tolman-style maze results suggest that animals can learn environmental structure rather than a single stimulus–response chain. When reward location changes or a familiar route closes, an agent with a transition map and reward model can plan before traversing every route again. A purely cached model-free Q estimate generally needs new prediction errors to change gradually.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Several mechanisms can rapidly alter choice, so this behavior does not uniquely identify a full map.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Spatial tuning neither establishes a complete model nor proves its use in the current choice.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Well-controlled revaluation experiments can constrain candidate learning mechanisms and representations.

conceptTags: Simulated experience, hippocampal replay, and sample efficiency
stem: Why is more replay not always better?

choices.text: Enough replay guarantees that systematic model errors cancel like independent zero-mean noise.
Each replay sample is a new independent observation of the real environment and therefore carries exactly the same new information as an actual trial.
More replay necessarily covers all state-action pairs uniformly, making sampling priorities irrelevant.
Repeated simulation from a biased model can reinforce wrong values; benefits also depend on coverage, priorities, and model uncertainty.

explanation: If the learned model has systematic error, repeated simulation amplifies its bias; coverage, priority, and model uncertainty must be balanced. Hippocampal replay reinstates place-cell sequences during rest or sleep. Sequences may run forward or backward, be temporally compressed, and favor reward or future paths. Replay is compatible with memory consolidation, planning, and credit propagation, but detecting a sequence does not show that downstream circuitry performs a particular numerical update; replay may serve several functions.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Repeatedly using a biased model does not automatically cancel its systematic error.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: A simulated sample comes from the existing model rather than a new observation of the environment.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Replay can repeatedly concentrate on a few experiences instead of improving coverage.

conceptTags: The agent–environment loop and a one-step Bellman backup
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “The agent–environment loop and a one-step Bellman backup”?

choices.text: The environment supplies reward and a successor state; a one-step target updates the current action value, and the successor starts the next interaction.
The Bellman backup directly changes environmental transition probabilities to force movement along the highest-value path.
Before choosing its action, the agent already observes that action's actual reward and successor state, so the illustrated target requires no environmental interaction.
Reward updates every action in the successor state while leaving the executed current action's value unchanged.

explanation: In the forward interaction, policy maps \(s_{t}\) to \(a_{t}\), after which the environment samples r and \(s_{t+1}\). The backup then uses \(r+\gamma \max_{a'}Q(s_{t+1},a')\) to update current \(Q(s_{t},a_{t})\). A dashed path carries \(s_{t+1}\) into the next cycle, showing that the Markov transition and value backup are connected steps pointing in opposite directions.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: The backup updates a value estimate rather than rewriting the environment's transition mechanism.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: The actual reward and successor are observed after the action and environmental response.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The illustrated update targets the value of the action actually taken in the current state.

conceptTags: Explicit memory, Hebbian assemblies, and pattern completion
stem: Why does \(m>0\) not guarantee successful retrieval?

choices.text: Positive overlap places a cue in the target basin by definition and guarantees success under every update order.
Overlap is the network's energy, so a positive value makes the target the unique global minimum.
Initial overlap depends only on how many patterns were stored and is completely independent of which cue bits were altered before retrieval.
Positive overlap indicates initial similarity to the target; retrieval still depends on the basin, crosstalk, and network conditions.

explanation: It measures only similarity at the start. The basin also depends on memory load, the particular crosstalk, update order, and network parameters. The Hebbian assembly hypothesis proposes that cells jointly active in an experience develop stronger mutual connections. Encoding changes the connections, a partial cue reactivates some members, and recurrent excitation recruits the missing members to complete the pattern. An engram is a cellular ensemble causally involved in memory storage and expression; activation correlation alone is insufficient for that label.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Overlap measures similarity, whereas a basin is determined by the full dynamics.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Overlap and energy are different quantities; positive overlap does not exclude other attractors.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Overlap directly compares the current cue with the target and changes with its particular errors.

conceptTags: Binary asynchronous dynamics and stored random patterns
stem: Why does updating every neuron once not guarantee a fixed point?

choices.text: Later updates can change the local fields of units updated earlier; another full sweep must check whether any state still changes.
Updating a unit permanently fixes its local field, so later changes in its neighbors cannot affect it.
A random update order guarantees that one sweep reaches the unique fixed point shared by every possible order.
Any energy decrease after one sweep proves that all units will remain unchanged thereafter, making further local-field checks unnecessary.

explanation: After an early unit is updated, later unit changes can alter its local field, so another complete sweep without changes is required. One sweep commonly means an average of N updates and does not imply convergence. Stop only after a full check finds no unit that would change or when both state and energy reach a fixed point. A finite deterministic asynchronous system under strict energy descent cannot visit new states forever, although arbitrary flipping on zero-field ties can create degeneracy.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: A local field depends on the current states of other units and can change when they update.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Random ordering guarantees neither one-sweep convergence nor a unique fixed point.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Energy may decrease during convergence; that alone does not establish a fixed point.

conceptTags: Energy descent and the \(P=1\) stored attractor
stem: Why does the derivation of \(\Delta E\) fail when W is asymmetric?

choices.text: Asymmetry only changes energy units, leaving every step of the original proof valid.
Asymmetric weights prevent the paired terms from yielding the update’s local field, invalidating the descent proof.
Asymmetry guarantees that every update raises energy, so all asymmetric networks must oscillate forever and can never reach any fixed state.
Asynchronous updates automatically turn any asymmetric matrix into an equivalent symmetric one.

explanation: Pair terms with i as the first and second index cannot be combined into the same local field, so one scalar energy need not decline under updating. Nonincreasing energy guarantees arrival at some local minimum, not the global minimum or target memory. A noisy cue may cross a basin boundary and reach a spurious state. Symmetric W is central to the proof. Asymmetric plasticity or delays can generate cycles, chaos, or sequential dynamics, so the same Lyapunov function cannot still be used to claim convergence.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Symmetry combines the pair terms in the energy difference; it is not a choice of units.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Losing a descent guarantee does not prove energy always rises or that every such network fails to converge.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The update schedule does not change the weight matrix's symmetry.

conceptTags: Spurious mixtures and the signal-plus-crosstalk decomposition
stem: Why does low mixture energy not make it a correct memory?

choices.text: Any state below the initial cue's energy should be redefined as that cue's correct memory.
Low mixture energy proves the complete mixture was presented as a training sample and could not have emerged from interactions among other stored patterns.
Energy describes dynamical stability, while correctness is defined by the stored target; a stable mixture may still be the wrong pattern.
The energy function carries explicit target labels and automatically rejects all unassigned stable states.

explanation: Correctness is defined by the training target and behavioral identity; energy determines dynamical stability and does not know which patterns were designated as memories. Basin boundaries shrink as P increases. A cue can have its highest overlap with the target and still flow to a mixture because all stored patterns jointly shape the energy landscape. Any analogy to experimental 'memory blending' is only a hypothesis; real memory distortion also depends on semantic inference, overlap during encoding, and systems consolidation.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Energy descent relative to the starting state cannot replace a check of target identity.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Crosstalk among stored patterns can create mixture attractors that were never stored individually.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The standard energy has no separate semantic label that identifies the intended target.

conceptTags: Gaussian crosstalk, loading, and classic capacity
stem: Why does \(\alpha =0.1\) below 0.138 still not guarantee success for every cue?

choices.text: Below critical load, every possible cue belongs to the desired basin, including cues identical to other stored memories.
The value 0.138 is an exact guarantee for any finite network, coding scheme, and tolerated retrieval error.
Once energy stops decreasing, the specified memory has necessarily been retrieved, so comparing the final state with the intended pattern is redundant.
The critical load is an asymptotic result under specific assumptions; finite networks, cue quality, and basin differences can cause failure.

explanation: The threshold is a large-N typical statistic under a particular retrieval criterion. Finite patterns, poor cues, basin differences, and random instances can still fail. For independent unbiased patterns, one nontarget overlap \(\sum _j\xi _{j}^{\mu }\xi _{j}^{1}\) has \(\operatorname{mean} 0\) and variance approximately N. After multiplication by 1/N, one pattern contributes field variance of about 1/N. Summing P-1 nearly independent terms gives crosstalk variance \((P-1)/N\approx \alpha\). This motivates a Gaussian-noise approximation through the central limit theorem.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Capacity does not guarantee retrieval of a specified target from every possible cue.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: The classical value depends on pattern statistics, the large-network limit, and the retrieval criterion.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Convergence to an incorrect or spurious attractor also stops updates; target identity must be checked separately.

conceptTags: Sparse stochastic associative memory and global inhibition
stem: Why does an uncentered 0/1 Hebbian rule produce a global positive bias?

choices.text: Uncentered coactivity adds only positive terms without negative cancellation from inactivity, potentially driving excessive activity.
Zeros in 0/1 patterns automatically create negative weights that cancel every positive coactivity term.
Sufficiently sparse patterns make every weight's mean exactly zero, so neither centering nor threshold control can ever be needed for stable activity.
The positive bias arises because the Hebbian rule counts only shared silence and ignores coactivity.

explanation: Only jointly active bits contribute positively, while inactivity supplies no canceling term. Across many patterns, most weights become positive and drive excessive activity. Place global inhibition directly in every weight by subtracting \(\gamma /(aN)\) after the centered Hebbian term. In the local field, this uniform negative term becomes \(-(\gamma /(aN))\sum _jS_{j}\), so a larger active population imposes stronger inhibition on every unit. Together with stochastic threshold u, it constrains total activity near aN. It is not one particular inhibitory neuron; rewriting it as an adaptive threshold requires an explicit mapping to population activity.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: A product containing zero is zero, not a negative contribution.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Sparsity does not imply zero mean; uncentered coactivity can retain a positive bias.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The positive contributions in the uncentered 0/1 outer product come from coactivity.

conceptTags: Hopfield basins: descent does not guarantee correct recall
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Hopfield basins: descent does not guarantee correct recall”?

choices.text: The path to the spurious attractor must contain an energy increase, or an incorrect memory would be unreachable.
Both paths can lower energy yet enter target and spurious basins respectively; dynamical convergence is therefore distinct from correct recall.
Because both paths use the same symmetric weights, every initial cue must end at one unique stored pattern, regardless of its similarity to other memories.
Minimum energy automatically identifies the requested target, making a stable mixture a correct recall.

explanation: With symmetric weights, a zero diagonal, and asynchronous updates, both paths make E nonincreasing, but the cue's basin determines the endpoint. A cue near the target can complete to \(\xi ^{\mu }\), whereas crosstalk may draw an ambiguous cue into a mixture. Energy descent, reaching a fixed point, and correct recall are distinct: low energy alone does not imply that the state is already stable, and a fixed point may encode a spurious memory.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Under symmetric asynchronous dynamics, a wrong attractor can also be reached without increasing energy.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: One network can have several basins, and the initial cue influences the final state.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Energy does not contain an independent label for the requested target identity.

conceptTags: Recent and remote memory, E.P., and evidence for systems consolidation
stem: Why does correct recall of facts from a remote memory not show that the original episode was preserved intact?

choices.text: Facts can come from semantic knowledge or reconstruction; preservation of original spatial, temporal, and perceptual details needs separate testing.
Correct remote facts prove that every sensory detail of the original episode remains intact.
Correct remote facts show complete independence from all medial temporal structures, and this conclusion must hold for every person and every memory task.
Using semantic knowledge to answer facts proves that no episodic memory was ever formed.

explanation: Facts can be reconstructed from semantic knowledge, rehearsal, or schemas; spatiotemporal and perceptual details must be tested separately. The standard systems-consolidation account holds that recent memory initially depends on hippocampal indexing. Through replay and reactivation, neocortical connections gradually become able to support retrieval. Temporally graded amnesia, hippocampal lesions, and remote knowledge provide evidence. This is not the movement of a physical memory file from one place to another; it is a reorganization of network dependence.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Factual knowledge and rich episodic detail are distinct aspects of memory performance.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: One performance measure does not establish every anatomical dependency or justify unrestricted generalization.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Current semantic support does not rule out a richer episodic representation in the past.

conceptTags: Teacher–Student–Notebook: three roles and the replay channel
stem: Why need Notebook replay not reproduce the original experience pixel for pixel?

choices.text: Replay can drive learning only by reproducing every original input pixel exactly, making all approximate targets useless.
Replay must recover targets or statistical structure needed by the Student; exact detail-by-detail fidelity depends on the model's assumptions.
Any Notebook activity necessarily teaches the correct rule, even if it preserves no task-relevant relationship at all.
During replay the Student must receive the identical online Teacher input again, because learning without the Teacher present is impossible by definition.

explanation: It can serve as a training sample as long as it reconstructs the task-relevant statistics or targets required for Student learning; the required fidelity is a modeling assumption. With only a slow Student, a rare experience may disappear before it is learned. With only a fast Notebook, episodes can be recalled accurately, but population regularities are difficult to extract and both capacity and interference remain limiting. Complementary timescales first write online experiences into the Notebook; later, interleaved replay mixes old and new samples for the Student and reduces the overwriting of old structure by new learning.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: A useful learning target need not reproduce every perceptual detail of the original experience.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Useful training still requires the relevant target or statistics; arbitrary activity provides no such guarantee.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The Notebook can supply reconstructed training samples while the Teacher is absent.

conceptTags: The autoassociative Notebook: separation, completion, and bidirectional connections
stem: Why is stronger pattern separation not always better?

choices.text: Stronger separation guarantees correct addressing from every partial cue, eliminating any need for pattern completion.
Maximum separation maps every experience to one identical sparse code so that replay can avoid all conflicts between memory addresses.
Excessive separation can impair retrieval from similar partial cues and consume code space, creating a tradeoff with completion.
Separation changes replay speed only and can never affect cue similarity, address reliability, or storage capacity.

explanation: If similar partial cues are mapped with no continuity, retrieval addresses become fragile; stronger separation also consumes finite code space. Separation and completion operate at different stages: encoding increases distances among episodes, whereas retrieval decreases the distance between a cue and a stored pattern within one basin. Excessive separation can prevent a partial cue from generalizing to the right address; excessive completion can force an ambiguous cue into the wrong episode. The two processes must balance capacity, specificity, and robustness.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: Reducing overlap between episodes does not guarantee that an incomplete cue reaches the right memory.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: One shared code increases confusion rather than separating episodes.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Separation changes representational geometry and can affect these retrieval and capacity properties.

conceptTags: The linear Teacher/Student model: memory error and generalization error
stem: Why can the minimum generalization error remain above zero?

choices.text: Recovering the true weights also predicts each new random noise realization exactly, forcing error to zero.
Any positive minimum error proves the optimizer has not converged, and continued fitting of stored examples must eventually eliminate every source of error.
Memorizing one episode's noise in the Notebook makes independent noise in every new episode predictable to the Student.
New targets contain unpredictable noise, so even recovery of the true weights leaves an irreducible component of generalization error.

explanation: The Teacher target contains unpredictable noise \(\epsilon\). Even if the Student recovers the true weight, it cannot predict \(\epsilon\) in a new episode. Experiments must assess training memory and generalization on different stimuli. Testing on the same episodes used for training measures only memory error and cannot establish schema learning. P, input dimensionality, noise variance, and learning time should also be reported because they determine when overfitting occurs.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: The true underlying rule does not specify an independent new noise realization.
wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Further training-set fitting cannot eliminate error from unpredictable new noise.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Memory for previously observed noise does not predict independent future noise.

conceptTags: Go-CLS: predictability, stopping consolidation, and lesion predictions
stem: Why does 'stopping consolidation' not mean deleting the Notebook memory?

choices.text: The Student stops further fitting that component; the Notebook may retain it and still support retrieval of episodic details.
Stopping consolidation requires immediate deletion of the component from the Notebook.
Stopping proves that the Student has copied every detail perfectly, making all future Notebook support for that component unnecessary.
Stopping consolidation halts the encoding and retrieval of every memory, not just transfer of the selected component to the Student.

explanation: What stops is further Student fitting of that component; the Notebook can still preserve it and support retrieval of episodic detail. Go-CLS defines the goal of consolidation as generalization, not complete copying of Notebook contents. Use the signal-to-noise-style quantity \(\lambda =E[(w_{\mathrm{T}}^\mathrm{T} x)^{2}]/E[\epsilon ^{2}]\). It can be simplified to a variance ratio only when predictable signal and noise have both been centered. With high \(\lambda\), cross-episode regularity is strong and the Student benefits from replay for longer. With low \(\lambda\), sample-specific detail dominates, the generalization optimum occurs earlier, and transfer should stop or weaken.

wrongChoiceExplanations.b: Stopping transfer and deleting an existing episodic record are different operations.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: The stopping point is based on generalization, not perfect copying of unpredictable detail.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: The model concerns transfer of a particular component, not shutdown of the entire memory system.

conceptTags: The offline replay channel in Teacher–Student–Notebook
stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “The offline replay channel in Teacher–Student–Notebook”?

choices.text: Offline replay must first obtain a fresh online Teacher sample; the Notebook cannot supply a learning target itself.
The Notebook completes the cue and reconstructs Student activity through the readout, enabling replay-based learning while the Teacher is absent.
The readout maps all Notebook codes to one identical activity pattern, so storing distinct episode–Student pairings is unnecessary for the depicted reconstruction.
Notebook completion proves the Student has learned the true environmental rule and needs no further update.

explanation: During online learning, Teacher generates training experiences, and each Student pattern \(z^{\mu }\) is stored together with its Notebook code \(\xi ^{\mu }\). During retrieval, the Notebook first completes a partial cue and then uses V to compute \(\widetilde{z}_i=\sum _jV_{ij}\xi _{j}\). The dashed replay path returns the reconstructed activity to Student, allowing Student to continue learning while Teacher is absent.

wrongChoiceExplanations.a: The illustrated replay path allows reconstructed activity to be used without the Teacher present.
wrongChoiceExplanations.c: Reconstruction depends on paired storage rather than collapsing every experience to one target.
wrongChoiceExplanations.d: Completion supplies a replay sample; learning a generalizable rule still depends on Student training.
